The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast. Estimating difficulty from limited probes Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability: success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½) Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards. We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass: Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper . One task, end to end Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update. Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band. When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1] . Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band. The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks. What earns a reward Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict. When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0. In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks. Two reward paths, one binary verdict Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed. Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test. Run the training stack We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training . The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are: docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting; docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration; docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv . You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency. The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark. Install Keep the three repositories side by side: mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1 git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 Create the validated environment The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606 python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install python scripts/verify_verl_install.py uv pip check The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel. Prepare the training data Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate python data/prepare_data.py -- help The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command. Configure and inspect the launch Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history. Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command: DRY_RUN= true ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run. Train The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray: # head node ROLE= head NODE_IP= " $HEAD_IP " GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh # each worker node ROLE=worker NODE_IP= " $WORKER_IP " \ HEAD_ADDRESS= " $HEAD_IP :6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node: export RAY_ADDRESS=auto export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \ trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md , then serve it with vLLM. From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration: vllm serve " $MERGED_MODEL " \ --served-model-name q38-rlft \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8001 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --language-model-only \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness: curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml ; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration: orchestrator: agent_model: type: aoai endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions deployment: q38-rlft credential: type: api-key api_key: <your_api_key> is_reasoning: true temperature: 1.0 top_k: 20 top_p: 0.95 max_completion_tokens: 8192 timeout: 1800 Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA . items.content: Back to Articles Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 28 +22 Fearghal O'Donncha Fearghal Follow ibm-research Chandramouli Kamanchi rry003 Follow ibm-research Guruprasad Ranjini Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Natalia Martinez Gil natalialmg91 Follow ibm-research Bradley Eck bradleyjeck Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use. Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task. Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed. The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast. Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face: pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11" import pandas as pd from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster df = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv" , parse_dates=[ "date" ], ) ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , ) result = ensemble( df.tail( 1024 ), timestamp_column= "date" , target_columns=[ "OT" ], context_length= 1024 , prediction_length= 24 , ) print (result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast print (result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card . result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage. The ensemble members The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures: Model Architecture Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer) For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper , PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview , FlowState paper , and Tiny Time Mixers paper . These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter. Two ways to combine the forecasts Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median. Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series. The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above. IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing. A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight. Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder: ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , subfolder= "recipes/granite-iqr" , ) Which method should I use? Your goal Start with Why A simple default Probabilistic Ensemble Equal influence, no fitted weights Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread IQR Ensemble Influence varies with each member's predicted spread Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon. Does the ensemble improve on its members? We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026. GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations. Lower is better. Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓ Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683 ★ 47.175 ★ 0.471 50.948 Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619 ★ Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467 ★ 48.918 Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485 Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134 Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959 ★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better. Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard. Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data. PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices. In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member. Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values. Extend the recipe to other forecasters The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve. The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them. For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing. Evaluate the recipe for your application GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data: Match your use case . Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve. Compare like with like . Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows. Look beyond point error . Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%. Measure the cost . Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload. Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment. Try it on your data The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe: Granite Timeseries Ensemble on Hugging Face Getting-started notebook Granite TSFM repository GIFT-Eval benchmark Load the default recipe to get median and quantile forecasts from all four Granite architectures in one call, and adapt the recipe as your needs evolve. References ECMWF: Ensemble weather forecasting NOAA: North American Multi-Model Ensemble FlowState: Sampling-Rate-Equivariant Time-Series Forecasting Tiny Time Mixers (TTMs): Fast Pre-trained Models for Enhanced Zero/Few-Shot Forecasting of Multivariate Time Series Revisiting the Generic Transformer: Deconstructing a Strong Baseline for Time Series Foundation Models Forecast combinations: an over 50-year review Smith and Wallis (2009), A Simple Explanation of the Forecast Combination Puzzle Models mentioned in this article 5 Spaces mentioned in this article 1 More from this author ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model 27 October 20, 2026 Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again? 123 September 15, 2026 Community Edit Preview Upload images, audio, and videos by dragging in the text input, pasting, or clicking here . Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values. Extend the recipe to other forecasters The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve. The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them. For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing. Evaluate the recipe for your application GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data: Match your use case . Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve. Compare like with like . Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows. Look beyond point error . Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%. Measure the cost . Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload. Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment. Try it on your data The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe: Granite Timeseries Ensemble on Hugging Face Getting-started notebook Granite TSFM repository GIFT-Eval benchmark Load the default recipe to get median and quantile forecasts from all four Granite architectures in one call, and adapt the recipe as your needs evolve. items.content: Back to Articles Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up Published October 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 34 +28 David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow In a previous post , we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do? The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself. Look up a model The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory. To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler ( neuronx-cc ) and of Transformers to look at. At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks. Run it yourself Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement : it loads the model with from_pretrained , sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron") . On a Trainium2 ( trn2 ) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container , install the packages, then run: python3 run.py No need for torchrun : the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded. A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version: hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache What "runs" means Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English. At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations. The results are a dataset Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions. Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet( "hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data" ) df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" ][[ "neuronx_cc" , "library" , "library_version" , "neuron_cores" , "result" ]] The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result. Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up . Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Anthony Maltsev amaltsev Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Brandon Brandon3967 Follow LiquidAI Samuel Stevens samuelstevens Follow LiquidAI Ryan Shubert shubeydoo Follow LiquidAI Tianshu Yu tianshu-yu Follow LiquidAI Sina s-jse Follow LiquidAI Tim Seyde tseyde Follow LiquidAI Rouzbeh Amin Tafreshi rouzbehat78 Follow LiquidAI Alexander Amini alexanderamini Follow LiquidAI Saniya Karwa saniyakarwa Follow LiquidAI Marc Harkonen haerski Follow LiquidAI Anna Piunova orech Follow LiquidAI Calder Katyal CalderKat Follow LiquidAI Ishwarya Ananthabhotla ianant93 Follow LiquidAI Farris Atif farris-liquid Follow LiquidAI Tarek Dakhran tdakhran Follow LiquidAI Paul Pak paulpak58 Follow LiquidAI xx tugot17 Follow LiquidAI Mihir Bafna mihirbafna Follow LiquidAI Kyle Bruce Wheeler m3m0ryh0l3 Follow LiquidAI Aditya Tadimeti adityatadimeti Follow LiquidAI Alfred Eng alfredeng Follow LiquidAI Karthik Macherla karthikrmacherla Follow LiquidAI Khoi Nguyen KTLK Follow LiquidAI Aldo Gael Carranza agcarranza Follow LiquidAI Aurelien Lac Aurelien-Lac Follow LiquidAI Tyler Murray undfined Follow LiquidAI Raahul Vignesh Raahul26 Follow LiquidAI Song Duong sduong Follow LiquidAI Ramin Hasani raminmh Follow LiquidAI Mathias Lechner mlech26l Follow LiquidAI Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare akhileshdeepakgotmare Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Jiahui Wang WWWjiahui Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI Alay Shah alay2shah Follow LiquidAI Simon Lee yungisimon Follow LiquidAI Mayank Agarwal mayankagarwal Follow LiquidAI Zetian Li zetianli Follow LiquidAI changyi yang changyiyang Follow LiquidAI Sinoué GAD GAD-cell Follow LiquidAI nathan ranchin nathanrchn Follow LiquidAI Sergei Tilga tilgasergey Follow LiquidAI LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs. LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family: More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters. Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model. Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device. Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment. How we built a more expressive backbone LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes: Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2. Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization. Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE. Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B . The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens. One backbone for six models Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device. Model Input Output Built on LFM3-1.7B Text Text LFM3-1.7B-Base LFM3-VL-2B Text, images, video Text LFM3 backbone + vision encoder LFM3-Audio-2B Text, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + audio encoder, audio decoder, and LiquidCodec LFM3-Omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + vision and audio encoders and audio decoder d1-2B Text, images, video Calibrated answers LFM3-VL-2B d1-omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Calibrated answers LFM3-Omni-2B The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders: Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length. Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding. How to use the LFM3 models Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. LFM3-1.7B Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers : pip install -U transformers Then load and run the model: from transformers import pipeline generator = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B" , trust_remote_code= True , ) messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is C. elegans?" }] output = generator( messages, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 2048 , ) print (output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ][ "content" ]) For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide . LFM3-VL-2B Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card . To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow Then load and run the model: import torch from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B" model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map= "auto" , trust_remote_code= True ) processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "url" : "https://placecats.com/300/200" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Describe this image." }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 16384 , # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True )[ 0 ]) See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp. LFM3-Audio-2B Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub: import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Respond with interleaved text and audio." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }]}, { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "<|mixed_start|>" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, continue_final_message= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , audio_temperature= 1.0 , audio_top_k= 128 , audio_repetition_penalty= 1.1 , audio_repetition_window= 4096 , return_dict_in_generate= True , ) text = processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) waveform = codec.decode( outputs.audio_codes[: 1 , :, :outputs.audio_lengths[ 0 ]] ).audio_values[ 0 ] # 24 kHz print (text) sf.write( "reply.wav" , waveform. float ().cpu().numpy(), 24_000 ) See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling. LFM3-Omni-2B Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card . To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch torchvision torchcodec accelerate pillow librosa soundfile import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question about a photo by voice: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Answer questions about the provided image. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Respond with text." , }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "photo.jpg" }, { "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , generation_mode= "text" ) print (processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:outputs.sequence_lengths[ 0 ]], skip_special_tokens= True , )) See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling. d1-2B and d1-omni-2B Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. Please refund one charge." , questions) a = out[ "answers" ] urgency = a[ "urgency" ][ "legend" ][ str ( int (a[ "urgency" ][ "score" ]))] print ( round (a[ "refund" ][ "noul" ], 2 ), a[ "team" ][ "choice" ], a[ "topics" ][ "choices" ], urgency) # 1.0 billing ['billing', 'delivery'] medium For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions. Fine-tune LFM3 for your task LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud. Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation. items.raw_text: Back to Articles Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3 Team Article Published October 27, 2026 Upvote 95 +89 Leonie Monigatti iamleonie Follow LiquidAI Jimmy T.H. Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Anthony Maltsev amaltsev Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Brandon Brandon3967 Follow LiquidAI Samuel Stevens samuelstevens Follow LiquidAI Ryan Shubert shubeydoo Follow LiquidAI Tianshu Yu tianshu-yu Follow LiquidAI Sina s-jse Follow LiquidAI Tim Seyde tseyde Follow LiquidAI Rouzbeh Amin Tafreshi rouzbehat78 Follow LiquidAI Alexander Amini alexanderamini Follow LiquidAI Saniya Karwa saniyakarwa Follow LiquidAI Marc Harkonen haerski Follow LiquidAI Anna Piunova orech Follow LiquidAI Calder Katyal CalderKat Follow LiquidAI Ishwarya Ananthabhotla ianant93 Follow LiquidAI Farris Atif farris-liquid Follow LiquidAI Tarek Dakhran tdakhran Follow LiquidAI Paul Pak paulpak58 Follow LiquidAI xx tugot17 Follow LiquidAI Mihir Bafna mihirbafna Follow LiquidAI Kyle Bruce Wheeler m3m0ryh0l3 Follow LiquidAI Aditya Tadimeti adityatadimeti Follow LiquidAI Alfred Eng alfredeng Follow LiquidAI Karthik Macherla karthikrmacherla Follow LiquidAI Khoi Nguyen KTLK Follow LiquidAI Aldo Gael Carranza agcarranza Follow LiquidAI Aurelien Lac Aurelien-Lac Follow LiquidAI Tyler Murray undfined Follow LiquidAI Raahul Vignesh Raahul26 Follow LiquidAI Song Duong sduong Follow LiquidAI Ramin Hasani raminmh Follow LiquidAI Mathias Lechner mlech26l Follow LiquidAI Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare akhileshdeepakgotmare Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Jiahui Wang WWWjiahui Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI Alay Shah alay2shah Follow LiquidAI Simon Lee yungisimon Follow LiquidAI Mayank Agarwal mayankagarwal Follow LiquidAI Zetian Li zetianli Follow LiquidAI changyi yang changyiyang Follow LiquidAI Sinoué GAD GAD-cell Follow LiquidAI nathan ranchin nathanrchn Follow LiquidAI Sergei Tilga tilgasergey Follow LiquidAI LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs. LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family: More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters. Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model. Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device. Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment. How we built a more expressive backbone LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes: Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2. Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization. Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE. Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B . The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens. One backbone for six models Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device. Model Input Output Built on LFM3-1.7B Text Text LFM3-1.7B-Base LFM3-VL-2B Text, images, video Text LFM3 backbone + vision encoder LFM3-Audio-2B Text, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + audio encoder, audio decoder, and LiquidCodec LFM3-Omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + vision and audio encoders and audio decoder d1-2B Text, images, video Calibrated answers LFM3-VL-2B d1-omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Calibrated answers LFM3-Omni-2B The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders: Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length. Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding. How to use the LFM3 models Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. LFM3-1.7B Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers : pip install -U transformers Then load and run the model: from transformers import pipeline generator = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B" , trust_remote_code= True , ) messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is C. elegans?" }] output = generator( messages, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 2048 , ) print (output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ][ "content" ]) For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide . LFM3-VL-2B Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card . To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow Then load and run the model: import torch from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B" model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map= "auto" , trust_remote_code= True ) processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "url" : "https://placecats.com/300/200" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Describe this image." }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 16384 , # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True )[ 0 ]) See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp. LFM3-Audio-2B Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub: import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Respond with interleaved text and audio." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }]}, { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "<|mixed_start|>" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, continue_final_message= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , audio_temperature= 1.0 , audio_top_k= 128 , audio_repetition_penalty= 1.1 , audio_repetition_window= 4096 , return_dict_in_generate= True , ) text = processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) waveform = codec.decode( outputs.audio_codes[: 1 , :, :outputs.audio_lengths[ 0 ]] ).audio_values[ 0 ] # 24 kHz print (text) sf.write( "reply.wav" , waveform. float ().cpu().numpy(), 24_000 ) See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling. LFM3-Omni-2B Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Respond with text." , }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "photo.jpg" }, { "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , generation_mode= "text" ) print (processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:outputs.sequence_lengths[ 0 ]], skip_special_tokens= True , )) See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling. d1-2B and d1-omni-2B Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. Until then, test out our latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.42139 (cs) [Submitted on 30 Oct 2026] Title: Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches Authors: Vitaly Feldman , Audra McMillan , Kunal Talwar View a PDF of the paper titled Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches, by Vitaly Feldman and Audra McMillan and Kunal Talwar View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: In many practical deployments of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), the server processes data in batches. Randomly sampling these batches allows for better privacy bounds via privacy amplification results. Most sampling schemes with provable privacy amplification, including Poisson sampling and random allocation, result in variable batch sizes. The privacy guarantee of these schemes requires that the batch sizes are not revealed. In distributed settings, the server performing the aggregation or any party observing the communication traffic may learn these batch sizes. Furthermore, in both centralized and distributed settings, memory and computation constraints may require each batch to be of some maximum size $s$, necessitating truncation of the batch when it exceeds this limit. It is known that this truncation can result in a significant increase in privacy loss. In this work, we address both of these challenges via a simple mechanism that uses a random number of \emph{dummy points} to privatize the batch size and maintain the privacy guarantee even under truncation. We demonstrate that our mechanism is easy to implement in a distributed setting, and provide a general analysis of this mechanism for both Poisson sampling and random allocation. Our analysis is designed to support efficient and relatively tight privacy accounting. It also effectively amplifies the privacy of the count releases by subsampling, making the expected number of dummy points asymptotically smaller than what is needed to directly privatize the (sensitivity-one) batch sizes with non-negative noise. For Poisson sampling with truncated batches, we demonstrate empirically that our mechanism achieves better privacy--efficiency tradeoffs than the direct accounting for truncation recently given by (Ganesh, 2025). items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.42133 (cs) [Submitted on 30 Oct 2026] Title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger Authors: Akshay Balsubramani View a PDF of the paper titled Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger, by Akshay Balsubramani View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes are proved by one chain. It runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimization over alternatives and allocations. Only the first step is an identity. This work writes the chain as an exact ledger. By the chain rule, data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at the per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances. The classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects. All defects but the asymptotic step's can be computed from an algorithm's own runs, the uniform quantification's only when the class guarantee is a number. On seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger locates the difference between standard algorithms and the classical limits. For identification among trained models and for Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification's. items.raw_text: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.42133 (cs) [Submitted on 30 Oct 2026] Title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger Authors: Akshay Balsubramani View a PDF of the paper titled Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger, by Akshay Balsubramani View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes are proved by one chain. It runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimization over alternatives and allocations. Only the first step is an identity. This work writes the chain as an exact ledger. By the chain rule, data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at the per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances. The classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects. All defects but the asymptotic step's can be computed from an algorithm's own runs, the uniform quantification's only when the class guarantee is a number. On seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger locates the difference between standard algorithms and the classical limits. For identification among trained models and for Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification's. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.42126 (cs) [Submitted on 30 Oct 2026] Title: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions Authors: Benjamin T. Pike View a PDF of the paper titled Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions, by Benjamin T. Pike View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Objective: To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity. Materials and Methods: In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant. Results: Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2-R1 log-loss difference -0.00922, 95% CI -0.01148 to -0.00704). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3-R2 -0.00257, 95% CI -0.00370 to -0.00146), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision (-0.00012, 95% CI -0.00206 to +0.00208). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful. Discussion: Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements. Conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs. Comments: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. items.content: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction : Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions Benjamin T. Pike Abstract Objective To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity. Materials and Methods In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant. Results Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2–R1 log-loss difference − 0.00922 -0.00922 , 95% CI − 0.01148 -0.01148 to − 0.00704 -0.00704 ). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3–R2 − 0.00257 -0.00257 , 95% CI − 0.00370 -0.00370 to − 0.00146 -0.00146 ), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision ( − 0.00012 -0.00012 , 95% CI − 0.00206 -0.00206 to + 0.00208 +0.00208 ). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful. Discussion Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements. Conclusion Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs. 1 Background and Significance Modern intensive care produces rich longitudinal records, with repeated physiological measurements capturing not only a patient’s current state but also how their condition evolves over time. The latest heart rate, blood pressure, creatinine, or lactate measurement offers only a snapshot of current physiology, whereas the preceding trajectory can reveal whether an abnormality is persistent, improving, or worsening. This longitudinal information is widely used for ICU mortality prediction, with models often drawing on repeated physiological and laboratory measurements collected during the early course of critical illness ( Silva et al., 2012 ; Harutyunyan et al., 2019 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . Large critical care datasets such as MIMIC and eICU allow these models to be developed and evaluated across different time periods, recording systems, and hospitals ( Johnson et al., 2016a ; Johnson et al., 2023 ; Pollard et al., 2018 ) . However, clinical records capture not only physiology but also how patients are observed. Similar recorded values may arise from very different measurement histories, differing in when and how often observations are made. Such differences may reflect clinical concern, treatment protocols, or local monitoring and documentation practices. Therefore, the resulting observation patterns can themselves carry predictive information, a phenomenon described as informative presence or informative observation ( Agniel et al., 2018 ; Sisk et al., 2021 ) . This information has also been incorporated directly into clinical time-series models such as GRU-D, which uses missingness and the time elapsed since previous observations as model inputs ( Che et al., 2018 ) . The extent to which this second source of predictive signal generalises across clinical settings is less certain. A patient’s physiological trajectory is expected to retain broadly similar meaning across settings, whereas the pattern by which that trajectory is observed is partly determined by the local environment. Models may therefore learn associations between measurement behaviour and outcome that are useful where they are developed but weaken or differ elsewhere. This concern has previously been described for informative missingness, where predictive performance depends on the stability of the underlying measurement process between development and deployment ( Groenwold, 2020 ) . More recent work found that observation-pattern features reduced the transportability of sepsis mortality models and added little beyond creatinine trajectories for ICU acute kidney injury prediction ( Yamamoto et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026 ) . Cross-setting differences in performance are challenging to interpret because several aspects of the data may change simultaneously: the patient population, the variables available, and when or how often they are recorded ( Riley et al., 2016 ; Pajouheshnia et al., 2019 ) . The predictive value of a longitudinal record may depend not only on how many observations it contains, but also on when they occur. The same number of measurements may be clustered near the time of prediction, separated by a period of sparse observation, or distributed across the preceding history. It remains unclear whether temporal placement matters independently of observation quantity and whether models that explicitly encode observation patterns are particularly sensitive to such differences. 2 Objective At a 48-hour ICU prediction landmark, the study addressed three primary questions. First, do longitudinal physiological summaries improve mortality prediction beyond a latest-value snapshot? Second, do observation patterns add further predictive information, and does that information persist across settings? Third, when the number of observations is held constant, does their placement in time affect performance? Subsequent local-development, explanatory, and adaptation analyses examined possible explanations for these differences and whether performance could be recovered when observation availability changed. 3 Materials and Methods 3.1 Prediction task and study overview The task was to predict in-hospital mortality 48 hours after ICU entry. Inputs comprised the ICU record available up to that point; patients with stays shorter than 48 hours were excluded from the prediction population. The study used MIMIC-III version 1.4, which spans the transition from the earlier CareVue system to MetaVision; MIMIC-IV version 3.1, which contains additional MetaVision data from the same institution; and eICU version 2.0, a multicentre database compiled through the Philips eICU programme ( Johnson et al., 2016b ; Johnson et al., 2024 ; Pollard et al., 2019 ) . Throughout, CareVue and MetaVision refer to the corresponding MIMIC-III cohorts, while MIMIC-IV is referred to separately. Nested representations progressively incorporated more of each patient’s record: first the latest recorded state, then longitudinal summaries of physiological severity, trajectory, and variability, and finally summaries of observation patterns. Generalisation within the same institution was evaluated across different recording periods and systems using the MIMIC datasets. Models were then fitted using all MetaVision patients and evaluated on MIMIC-IV and eICU using the same harmonised feature set. Subsequent restriction experiments removed observations from each patient’s record and rebuilt the representations, varying both how many observations were retained and when during the 48-hour window they occurred. 3.2 Populations and evaluation settings All cohorts were restricted to patients aged 18 years or older. The CareVue cohort comprised 12,518 eligible patients. Models were fitted on the complete cohort and evaluated on all 7,762 eligible MetaVision patients. MIMIC-IV ICU stays were restricted to those whose earliest possible calendar year was 2013 or later to avoid overlap with the MIMIC-III recording period. MetaVision models were trained on all 7,762 eligible patients and evaluated on all 21,682 eligible MIMIC-IV patients. Complete selection details are provided in the Supplementary Material. Within each source cohort, all representations used the same five outcome-stratified folds for internal evaluation and out-of-fold calibration. Final source models were fitted on the complete eligible cohort. Local eICU hospital-grouped cross-validation was repeated across 20 allocations, with performance and paired effects averaged equally across allocations. The eICU cohort additionally required a recorded hospital outcome. One hospital admission was selected per person, followed by the earliest ICU stay within that admission, after which eligibility was assessed. The cohort comprised 54,787 patients across 205 hospitals, of which 10,909 were reserved for supporting adaptation and 43,878 across 204 hospitals for external testing. Calibration and test sets were disjoint, although the same hospitals could contribute to both. Cohort details are shown in Table 1 . Table 1: Eligible MIMIC cohorts and the eICU evaluation population. Age is reported as median (interquartile range) in years. CareVue, MetaVision, and MIMIC-IV relate to the same institution. Seven eICU test records have sex outside the female/male categories shown. The separate 10,909-patient adaptation population is not included. Cohort Patients Deaths (%) Age Female Hospitals CareVue 12,518 1,733 (13.8) 67 (53–78) 5,488 1 MetaVision 7,762 1,005 (12.9) 66 (54–79) 3,485 1 MIMIC-IV 21,682 2,978 (13.7) 67 (56–77) 9,387 1 eICU 43,878 5,393 (12.3) 66 (55–77) 19,909 204 For the external analysis, the representation hierarchy and harmonisation decisions were fixed before eICU performance was examined. Models trained on the MetaVision cohort were applied to the MIMIC-IV and eICU evaluation cohorts without further tuning or refitting. Later explanatory and adaptation analyses were conducted after the initial external results were known and are therefore treated as post-hoc supporting analyses. Models trained within eICU were evaluated using hospital-grouped folds to distinguish poor transfer from a lack of locally useful information. 3.3 Model inputs and representations The five nested representations (R0–R4) are shown in Table 2 . R0 provides a minimal baseline. R1 is a snapshot of the patient’s state at 48 hours, based largely on the latest recorded values and other scalar inputs. R2 adds longitudinal summaries of physiological severity, trend, and variability, forming the trajectory representation. R3 additionally describes how the patient was observed, including how often and when measurements were recorded. R4 adds a broader set of physiological and observation summaries. Each tier contains the preceding tier. Table 2: Nested information representations. Feature counts are reported before categorical variables are expanded during encoding. Shared counts indicate the subset retained after harmonisation between MetaVision and eICU. Tier Interpretation MIMIC Shared Information added R0 Baseline 10 10 Static inputs and latest values of six physiological variables. R1 Snapshot 43 42 Additional scalar values, urine output, and ventilation indicators. R2 Trajectory 335 334 Physiological severity, trend, and variability summaries. R3 Observation patterns 524 514 Measurement frequency, timing, and observation-pattern summaries. R4 Rich summary 940 918 Additional physiological and observation summaries. The R2–R1 comparison examines whether longitudinal physiological information improves prediction beyond the latest recorded state. The R3–R2 comparison assesses whether information about how and when measurements were recorded adds further predictive value. Given that each tier changes the size and structure of the model input, affecting interactions and regularisation, these comparisons assess the added value of each representation as a whole rather than the isolated effect of the newly added features. For external transfer, variables were harmonised between MetaVision and eICU using reviewed mappings of database tables, variable definitions, and units. Models using the shared feature set were fitted on MetaVision and evaluated in both MIMIC-IV and eICU. Because no equivalent eICU definition of a ventilation episode could be established, ventilation and dependent predictors were excluded from the shared representations rather than inferred. Complete feature definitions, mappings, missingness rules, and exclusions are provided in the Supplementary Material. 3.4 Observation restriction and timing analyses Observation restrictions were applied by removing selected recorded measurements, after which all summaries and derived predictors were rebuilt.
