Pike Abstract Objective To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity. Materials and Methods In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant. Results Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2–R1 log-loss difference − 0.00922 -0.00922 , 95% CI − 0.01148 -0.01148 to − 0.00704 -0.00704 ). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3–R2 − 0.00257 -0.00257 , 95% CI − 0.00370 -0.00370 to − 0.00146 -0.00146 ), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision ( − 0.00012 -0.00012 , 95% CI − 0.00206 -0.00206 to + 0.00208 +0.00208 ). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful. Discussion Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements. Conclusion Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs. 1 Background and Significance Modern intensive care produces rich longitudinal records, with repeated physiological measurements capturing not only a patient’s current state but also how their condition evolves over time. The latest heart rate, blood pressure, creatinine, or lactate measurement offers only a snapshot of current physiology, whereas the preceding trajectory can reveal whether an abnormality is persistent, improving, or worsening. This longitudinal information is widely used for ICU mortality prediction, with models often drawing on repeated physiological and laboratory measurements collected during the early course of critical illness ( Silva et al., 2012 ; Harutyunyan et al., 2019 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . Large critical care datasets such as MIMIC and eICU allow these models to be developed and evaluated across different time periods, recording systems, and hospitals ( Johnson et al., 2016a ; Johnson et al., 2023 ; Pollard et al., 2018 ) . However, clinical records capture not only physiology but also how patients are observed. Similar recorded values may arise from very different measurement histories, differing in when and how often observations are made. Such differences may reflect clinical concern, treatment protocols, or local monitoring and documentation practices. Therefore, the resulting observation patterns can themselves carry predictive information, a phenomenon described as informative presence or informative observation ( Agniel et al., 2018 ; Sisk et al., 2021 ) . This information has also been incorporated directly into clinical time-series models such as GRU-D, which uses missingness and the time elapsed since previous observations as model inputs ( Che et al., 2018 ) . The extent to which this second source of predictive signal generalises across clinical settings is less certain. A patient’s physiological trajectory is expected to retain broadly similar meaning across settings, whereas the pattern by which that trajectory is observed is partly determined by the local environment. Models may therefore learn associations between measurement behaviour and outcome that are useful where they are developed but weaken or differ elsewhere. This concern has previously been described for informative missingness, where predictive performance depends on the stability of the underlying measurement process between development and deployment ( Groenwold, 2020 ) . More recent work found that observation-pattern features reduced the transportability of sepsis mortality models and added little beyond creatinine trajectories for ICU acute kidney injury prediction ( Yamamoto et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026 ) . Cross-setting differences in performance are challenging to interpret because several aspects of the data may change simultaneously: the patient population, the variables available, and when or how often they are recorded ( Riley et al., 2016 ; Pajouheshnia et al., 2019 ) . The predictive value of a longitudinal record may depend not only on how many observations it contains, but also on when they occur. The same number of measurements may be clustered near the time of prediction, separated by a period of sparse observation, or distributed across the preceding history. It remains unclear whether temporal placement matters independently of observation quantity and whether models that explicitly encode observation patterns are particularly sensitive to such differences. 2 Objective At a 48-hour ICU prediction landmark, the study addressed three primary questions. First, do longitudinal physiological summaries improve mortality prediction beyond a latest-value snapshot? Second, do observation patterns add further predictive information, and does that information persist across settings? Third, when the number of observations is held constant, does their placement in time affect performance? Subsequent local-development, explanatory, and adaptation analyses examined possible explanations for these differences and whether performance could be recovered when observation availability changed. 3 Materials and Methods 3.1 Prediction task and study overview The task was to predict in-hospital mortality 48 hours after ICU entry. We show that the dynamics are organized by two directions: the "easy" bisector direction, which carries the leading signal, and the "hard" splitting direction, which governs specialization. Gradient Descent on Two ReLU Neurons: Global Landscape and Bifurcation Dynamics Binghua Li Mengzhe Li University of California, Berkeley École Normale Supérieure Paris-Saclay binghuali@berkeley.edu mengzhe.li_mengzhe@ens-paris-saclay.fr Denny Wu Tianhao Wang New York University & Flatiron Institute University of California, San Diego dwu@flatironinstitute.org tianhaowang@ucsd.edu Abstract Understanding how gradient descent learns features remains a central challenge in neural network theory. We study this question in a minimal multi-index setting that already exhibits rich multi-phase gradient dynamics: a well-specified two-neuron ReLU teacher-student model under isotropic Gaussian inputs, trained by population gradient flow from small initialization. We show that the dynamics are organized by two directions: the “easy” bisector direction, which carries the leading signal, and the “hard” splitting direction, which governs specialization. To characterize the loss structure and learning behavior, we analyze the population squared-loss landscape and show that every critical point with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle. We then track the gradient-flow trajectory, showing that student neurons first collapse toward a bisector saddle before escaping and specializing to teacher neurons. Our results provide both a landscape and dynamics account of the multi-phase symmetry-breaking behavior that arises in a simple multi-index model and under standard algorithmic and architectural choices. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 1 Introduction A central promise of gradient-based training of neural networks is feature learning : rather than fitting the target function on a fixed feature space, neural networks can extract features by aligning their parameters with the latent structure of the data or target function. A recent line of theoretical works has made this intuition precise by analyzing teacher-student models under Gaussian inputs, where the target function is a multi-index model ( Abbe et al., 2022 ; Damian et al., 2022 ; Ba et al., 2022 ) which depends on a small number of input directions (e.g., a shallow neural network with O d ​ ( 1 ) O_{d}(1) neurons). In these settings, it has been demonstrated that gradient descent training of a shallow “student” neural network discovers the relevant subspace, and achieves a sample complexity superior to fixed features methods (or neural networks in the “lazy” regime ( Chizat et al., 2019 ) ). However, most existing theory becomes tractable only after imposing simplifying assumptions that deviate from standard algorithmic and architectural choices. Examples include ( i ) (i) near-orthogonal teacher neurons ( Li et al., 2020 ; Ren and Lee, 2025 ) , ( i ​ i ) (ii) local convergence conditions ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) , ( i ​ i ​ i ) (iii) activation functions with high information exponent ( Oko et al., 2024 ; Şimşek et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2025 ) , and ( i ​ v ) (iv) modified algorithms such as loss preprocessing ( Damian et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) and spherical/Stiefel gradients ( Ben Arous et al., 2021 ; Ben Arous et al., 2026 ; Abbe et al., 2023 ) . While these assumptions enable clean analyses, they do not capture the complex multi-phase learning dynamics present in standard ReLU networks ( Boursier et al., 2022 ; Wang and Ma, 2023 ; Min et al., 2025 ) . A notable multi-index example exhibiting such nontrivial dynamics is the “well-specified” setting in which both the student and teacher are two-layer neural networks with matching activation functions and more than one neuron: for commonly used nonlinearities such as ReLU, the optimization trajectory exhibits symmetry-breaking and bifurcation behavior, with neurons initially moving toward an “average” direction before specializing to different teacher directions. While this plateau-specialization phenomenon has appeared in the statistical physics literature ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ; Goldt et al., 2020 ) , it is not captured by recent analyses that rely on the above simplifications. To our knowledge, a rigorous and quantitative understanding of the loss landscape and multi-phase training dynamics remains incomplete and largely open. 1.1 Our contributions We study arguably the simplest multi-index model setting that exhibits this bifurcation phenomenon: learning a two-neuron ReLU network under isotropic Gaussian inputs via population gradient flow, starting from small initialization. Specifically, the teacher model is f ∗ ​ ( x ) = ReLU ⁡ ( ⟨ v 1 , x ⟩ ) + ReLU ⁡ ( ⟨ v 2 , x ⟩ ) , x ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) , f^{*}(x)=\mathrm{ReLU}(\langle v_{1},xangle)+\mathrm{ReLU}(\langle v_{2},xangle),\qquad x\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_{d}), (1.1) where ReLU ⁡ ( z ) = max ⁡ { z , 0 } \mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max\{z,0\} , ‖ v 1 ‖ 2 = ‖ v 2 ‖ 2 = 1 \|v_{1}\|_{2}=\|v_{2}\|_{2}=1 and ∠ ⁡ ( v 1 , v 2 ) = α ∈ ( 0 , π 2 ] \angle(v_{1},v_{2})=\alpha\in(0, rac{\pi}{2}] , and the student has the same architecture with trainable weights w 1 , w 2 w_{1},w_{2} . v 1 + v 2 v_{1}+v_{2} (leap-1) v 1 − v 2 v_{1}-v_{2} (leap-2) v 1 v_{1} v 2 v_{2} w s w_{s} 0 0 Phase 1 (collapse) Phase 2 (split) student w 1 w_{1} student w 2 w_{2} teacher v i v_{i} saddle w s w_{s} Figure 1 : Illustration of bifurcation dynamics. As we will see, the geometry of this model is organized by two directions in the teacher plane: the bisector ( v 1 + v 2 v_{1}+v_{2} ), which carries the dominant signal, and the difference ( v 1 − v 2 v_{1}-v_{2} ), which governs specialization. In the language of leap complexity for Gaussian multi-index models ( Abbe et al., 2023 ; Bietti et al., 2025 ) , the target function ( 1.1 ) has leap exponent 2 2 , where the bisector and difference vectors specify the “easy” leap-1 direction and the “hard” leap-2 direction, respectively. This suggests a two-stage picture for gradient-based learning: the student neurons are first attracted toward the leap-1 bisector, and only later separate toward the individual teacher directions along the leap-2 direction. Our goal is to make this collapse-then-splitting picture quantitative by studying both the population squared loss landscape and the gradient-flow dynamics from small initialization. Specifically, • Landscape analysis. Section 3 studies the loss geometry and the critical-point structure for both the correlation loss and the MSE loss. We reduce the stationarity conditions to a three-dimensional problem and isolate the remaining in-plane and out-of-plane critical families. We establish that every critical point of the population loss with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle, so none of these critical points is a spurious local minimum. This resolves a two-neuron conjecture from Tian (2017) in the acute angle ( α ≤ π / 2 \alpha\leq\pi/2 ) setting. • Small-initialization dynamics. Section 4 studies the gradient-flow trajectory from small initialization and characterizes the symmetry breaking and specialization behavior — see Figure 1 . We show that for sufficiently small initialization, both student neurons stay close to the bisector for fixed finite time and approach the symmetric saddle. We then analyze escape from that saddle, including global convergence to a minimum for typical initializations, as well as a quantitative escape-time bound that is logarithmic in the ambient dimension d d with a structured initialization. 1.2 Further related work Learning multi-index models. Recent works have shown shallow neural networks can efficiently learn low-dimensional latent structure via gradient descent ( Abbe et al., 2022 ; Damian et al., 2022 ; Ba et al., 2022 ; Bietti et al., 2022 ; Glasgow, 2024 ; Dandi et al., 2024 ) . Specifically, the sample complexity has been shown to be superior to that of kernel methods and to be governed by the information exponent ( Dudeja and Hsu, 2018 ; Ben Arous et al., 2021 ) for single-index models and the leap exponent ( Abbe et al., 2023 ; Bietti et al., 2025 ) for multi-index models. Our target function ( 1.1 ) is an example of a leap-2 multi-index model, but, crucially, it also contains a leap-1 subspace, which complicates the SGD dynamics. In fact, most prior works studying gradient-based feature learning either directly assume link functions with information exponent 2 ( Li et al., 2020 ; Martin et al., 2024 ; Ren and Lee, 2025 ; Ben Arous et al., 2025 ) or higher ( Oko et al., 2024 ; Şimşek et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2025 ) , or remove the low-leap components through algorithmic modifications such as deflation / projection ( Ge et al., 2021 ; Abbe et al., 2023 ) and loss preprocessing ( Damian et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Consequently, these analyses do not fully characterize the learning dynamics of two ReLU neurons with standard gradient-based training. Training dynamics of ReLU networks. Restricting to shallow neural networks with ReLU activations, prior works have studied landscape properties such as the existence of spurious minima ( Safran and Shamir, 2018 ; Safran et al., 2021 ) ; the concurrent work of Huang et al. (2026) gives a summary-statistics characterization of the population minima and proposes an ansatz to simplify the fixed-point equations. For gradient-based training dynamics, while the single-neuron case is relatively well-understood ( Tian, 2017 ; Soltanolkotabi, 2017 ; Yehudai and Shamir, 2020 ; Xu and Du, 2023 ) , when the target network contains more than one neuron, existing dynamical analyses either assume local convergence, thereby bypassing the bifurcation behavior ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) , or require exponential width to invoke mean-field global convergence ( Chizat, 2022 ; Akiyama and Suzuki, 2021 ) . The two-phase trajectory illustrated in Figure 1 also relates to the “plateau” phenomenon observed in the statistical mechanics literature ( Biehl et al., 1996 ; Fukumizu and Amari, 2000 ) . Specifically, the specialization phenomenon has been investigated in Goldt et al. (2020) ; Oostwal et al. (2021) using the ODE analysis originated from Saad and Solla (1995) ; Riegler and Biehl (1995) . However, to our knowledge, a complete understanding of the landscape and rigorous characterization of the learning dynamics have not yet been established even in the two-neuron setting ( 1.1 ) studied here. 2 Preliminary Notation. Gradient Descent on Two ReLU Neurons: Global Landscape and Bifurcation Dynamics Binghua Li Mengzhe Li University of California, Berkeley École Normale Supérieure Paris-Saclay binghuali@berkeley.edu mengzhe.li_mengzhe@ens-paris-saclay.fr Denny Wu Tianhao Wang New York University & Flatiron Institute University of California, San Diego dwu@flatironinstitute.org tianhaowang@ucsd.edu Abstract Understanding how gradient descent learns features remains a central challenge in neural network theory. We study this question in a minimal multi-index setting that already exhibits rich multi-phase gradient dynamics: a well-specified two-neuron ReLU teacher-student model under isotropic Gaussian inputs, trained by population gradient flow from small initialization. We show that the dynamics are organized by two directions: the “easy” bisector direction, which carries the leading signal, and the “hard” splitting direction, which governs specialization. To characterize the loss structure and learning behavior, we analyze the population squared-loss landscape and show that every critical point with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle. We then track the gradient-flow trajectory, showing that student neurons first collapse toward a bisector saddle before escaping and specializing to teacher neurons. Our results provide both a landscape and dynamics account of the multi-phase symmetry-breaking behavior that arises in a simple multi-index model and under standard algorithmic and architectural choices. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 1 Introduction A central promise of gradient-based training of neural networks is feature learning : rather than fitting the target function on a fixed feature space, neural networks can extract features by aligning their parameters with the latent structure of the data or target function. A recent line of theoretical works has made this intuition precise by analyzing teacher-student models under Gaussian inputs, where the target function is a multi-index model ( Abbe et al., 2022 ; Damian et al., 2022 ; Ba et al., 2022 ) which depends on a small number of input directions (e.g., a shallow neural network with O d ​ ( 1 ) O_{d}(1) neurons). In these settings, it has been demonstrated that gradient descent training of a shallow “student” neural network discovers the relevant subspace, and achieves a sample complexity superior to fixed features methods (or neural networks in the “lazy” regime ( Chizat et al., 2019 ) ). However, most existing theory becomes tractable only after imposing simplifying assumptions that deviate from standard algorithmic and architectural choices. Examples include ( i ) (i) near-orthogonal teacher neurons ( Li et al., 2020 ; Ren and Lee, 2025 ) , ( i ​ i ) (ii) local convergence conditions ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) , ( i ​ i ​ i ) (iii) activation functions with high information exponent ( Oko et al., 2024 ; Şimşek et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2025 ) , and ( i ​ v ) (iv) modified algorithms such as loss preprocessing ( Damian et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) and spherical/Stiefel gradients ( Ben Arous et al., 2021 ; Ben Arous et al., 2026 ; Abbe et al., 2023 ) . While these assumptions enable clean analyses, they do not capture the complex multi-phase learning dynamics present in standard ReLU networks ( Boursier et al., 2022 ; Wang and Ma, 2023 ; Min et al., 2025 ) . A notable multi-index example exhibiting such nontrivial dynamics is the “well-specified” setting in which both the student and teacher are two-layer neural networks with matching activation functions and more than one neuron: for commonly used nonlinearities such as ReLU, the optimization trajectory exhibits symmetry-breaking and bifurcation behavior, with neurons initially moving toward an “average” direction before specializing to different teacher directions. While this plateau-specialization phenomenon has appeared in the statistical physics literature ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ; Goldt et al., 2020 ) , it is not captured by recent analyses that rely on the above simplifications. To our knowledge, a rigorous and quantitative understanding of the loss landscape and multi-phase training dynamics remains incomplete and largely open. 1.1 Our contributions We study arguably the simplest multi-index model setting that exhibits this bifurcation phenomenon: learning a two-neuron ReLU network under isotropic Gaussian inputs via population gradient flow, starting from small initialization. items.summary: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.42147 (cs) [Submitted on 30 Oct 2026] Title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention Authors: Ales Kubicek , Andrea Caciolai , Liangzu Peng , Sukrit Sumant , Benjamin Hoover , Fraser Greenlee , Ruairidh M. Battleday , Radim Urban , Torsten Hoefler , James C.R. Whittington View a PDF of the paper titled Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention, by Ales Kubicek and 9 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention Ales Kubicek * 1 Andrea Caciolai * 1 Liangzu Peng * 1 Sukrit Sumant 1 Benjamin Hoover 1 Fraser Greenlee 1 Ruairidh M. Battleday 1 Radim Urban 2 Torsten Hoefler 2 James C.R. Whittington † 1 † † footnotetext: * Core contributors. † Senior author. 1 Prefrontal AI, London, United Kingdom 2 ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland. Correspondence to: Ales Kubicek <ales@prefrontal.ai>, James C.R. Whittington <james@prefrontal.ai>. Preprint. Abstract Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-Flash ( Qwen-3.8-27B ) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7 × 22.7\times ( 72.4 × 72.4\times ) in prefill and 4.6 × 4.6\times ( 42.5 × 42.5\times ) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6 × 1.6\times per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context. 1 Introduction Figure 1: D-LSA and N-LSA overview. Top: one attention layer. The keys are pooled and clustered into buckets. A query ( ) scores the bucket centroids ( ) and attends only to the selected long-range keys (plus sink and window). Bottom: accuracy and performance (P: prefill, D: decode, T: training) for both D-LSA and N-LSA. D-LSA is shown with flat search. Its subquadratic variant, D-LSA (Tree), follows a similar trend (Figure 5 ). Large language models have moved from answering single requests to agentic workflows in long-horizon tasks, such as software engineering and open-ended scientific research ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . These tasks keep growing in length ( Kwa et al., 2025 ) , and models with longer context windows tend to score higher on them ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . In line with this trend, recent models extend their context windows to 1M tokens and beyond ( Gemini Team, 2024 ; MiniMax, 2025 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026a ; Qwen Team, 2026a ) . At this context size, attention dominates the cost, as its work grows with context ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Dao et al., 2022 ) . An established technique to reduce such costs is sparse attention ( Hoefler et al., 2021 ) , in which each query attends to only a subset of the keys, chosen by a fixed pattern ( Child et al., 2019 ; Beltagy et al., 2020 ; Zaheer et al., 2020 ) , by their content ( Kitaev et al., 2020 ; Roy et al., 2021 ) , or by a dedicated indexer ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Recent frontier models are increasingly adopting sparse attention, in which keys are selected using a dedicated indexer ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Qwen Team, 2026a ) . However, current indexers still score every preceding key, or block of keys, for each query. This remains expensive (quadratic in prefill, linear in decode), and becomes a bottleneck at long context ( Zan et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . For example, at 10M tokens, 98% of the prefill time of a sparse attention layer is spent on indexing (Figure 2 ). The cost of sparse attention at ultra-long context is therefore dominated by the cost of finding the keys. To address this, we introduce Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), which clusters keys in a learned latent space and lets each query search the clusters instead of scoring every key. This can be done using only one level of clustering ( Flat ), or with a hierarchy of clusters ( Tree ), which makes the prefill subquadratic. Furthermore, we propose two trainable designs: D-LSA, which adds LSA to pre-trained models and only trains small projection matrices per layer (contribution #1) , and N-LSA, which trains LSA natively with the Next-Token Prediction (NTP) loss alone (contribution #2) . We evaluate state-of-the-art models ( Qwen-3.8-27B and GLM-5.3-Flash ) beyond their advertised context, up to 10M tokens (contribution #3) , on RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) , which is an established long-context benchmark, and PaperTrail, which we developed to test long-context scientific understanding by finding and connecting facts across unseen scientific papers (contribution #4) . Finally, we integrate LSA into SGLang ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) 1 1 1 github.com/Prefrontal-AI/sglang with context parallelism, provide GPU kernels for H200 and B300, and release the code 2 2 2 github.com/Prefrontal-AI/latent-sparse-attention with all training and inference details (contribution #5) . Figure 1 outlines our contributions. 2 Sparse Attention In full attention, every query attends to every preceding key. Prefilling a context of T T tokens therefore costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( T 2 ) \mathcal{O}(T^{2}) , and decoding one token costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(T) . In sparse attention, the work is split between an indexer and the attention. For each query, the indexer selects which keys the attention attends to 3 3 3 In this view, full attention corresponds to an indexer that returns the indices of all preceding keys. . With a fixed budget of k k keys, the attention then costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ k ) \mathcal{O}(Tk) to prefill and 𝒪 ⁡ ( k ) \mathcal{O}(k) per decoded token. If the indexer selects the most relevant keys, this is sufficient to stay close to the accuracy of full attention (Appendix A ). However, the indexer has a cost. Since it must score all preceding keys, it typically remains 𝒪 ⁡ ( T 2 ) \mathcal{O}(T^{2}) in prefill and 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(T) in decode, though with reduced constant factors. This makes ultra-long context still prohibitively expensive. For example, at 10M tokens the indexer takes 98% of the prefill time of traditional sparse attention (Figure 2 ), and a ‘free’ indexer would make sparse attention a further 58 × 58\times faster in prefill and 8.9 × 8.9\times in decode. Figure 2: Traditional sparse attention at ultra-long context. One global attention layer of GLM-5.3-Flash (512k to 10M tokens) on one H200, prefilling the last chunk of 32,768 queries and decoding one token. Speedup of sparse attention over full attention ( blue ), share of the indexer ( % ), and potential speedup over sparse attention if the indexer were ‘free’ ( green ). 2.1 Design Choices Sparse attention methods can be categorised by their indexer designs and how they are trained. Token Sparse Attention. For each query, a lightweight indexer (fewer heads, smaller dimension, lower precision) scores every preceding key and selects which to attend to. Block Sparse Attention. Consecutive keys are grouped into blocks, and each query scores blocks instead of every key. All keys of the selected blocks are sent to the attention. Semantic Sparse Attention. Keys are clustered by similarity rather than position, and each query scores one centroid per cluster. All keys of the selected clusters are sent to the attention. For the last two categories, a query can search the groups in three ways. Flat search scores every group directly, which is 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(T) work per query. Fixed search adds a shallow hierarchy and refines from coarse to fine groups, which is also 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(T) per query. Tree search descends a deeper hierarchy and expands only the groups it keeps at each level, which is 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) \mathcal{O}(\log T) per query. An indexer can be training-free, distilled from a pre-trained model, or trained natively on the NTP loss alone. 2.2 Related Work Table 1: Sparse attention methods compared. Rows are grouped by the unit the indexer scores: single keys, blocks of consecutive keys, or clusters of similar keys. Design column: compression of the sequence the indexer scans by compressing consecutive keys (C. Seq.), or clustering keys by content (C. Sem.), and its search: flat ( ), a fixed number of levels ( ), or levels efficiently growing as log ⁡ T \log T ( ). Evaluation : the largest context at which accuracy (Acc.) and performance (Perf.) are reported. supported, partial support, not supported. Training Speedup Design Evaluation Name Free Distilled Native Prefill Decode C. Seq. C. Sem. Search Acc. Perf. Token Sparse Attention DSA ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) 128k 128k MiniMax SA ( Lai et al., 2026 ) 128k 1M Block Sparse Attention CSA ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026a ) 1M 1M QSA ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) 1M 1M GLM-5.3-Flash SA ( Z.ai, 2026 ) 1M 1M NSA ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) 64k 64k HSA-UltraLong ( Hu et al., 2026b ) 16M 256k MoBA ( Lu et al., 2025 ) 1M 10M SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) 128k 128k LongCat LSA ( Zan et al., 2026 ) 1M 1M HISA ( Xu et al., 2026 ) 128k 128k HiP ( Lee et al., 2025a ) 128k 512k PISA ( Tang et al., 2026 ) 16k 256k Semantic Sparse Attention ClusterKV ( Liu et al., 2025b ) 32k 32k RetroInfer ( Chen et al., 2026 ) 1M 1M Squeezed Attention ( Hooper et al., 2025b ) 32k 512k Multipole Attention ( Hooper et al., 2025a ) 128k 128k LycheeCluster ( Li et al., 2026 ) 128k 72k IceCache ( Mao et al., 2026b ) 250k 300k LSA 10M 10M Table 1 provides an overview of the existing work on sparse attention, as categorised above. We focus on methods that keep the whole KV cache and select keys per query, unlike fixed sparse patterns ( Child et al., 2019 ; Beltagy et al., 2020 ; Zaheer et al., 2020 ) and KV cache eviction techniques ( Zhang et al., 2023b ; Li et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2024b ) . Among distillation methods, DSA ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) and MiniMax SA ( Lai et al., 2026 ) first distil the indexer and then continue training the full model under sparse attention. Alternatively, SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) distils a gate over pooled blocks and HashAttention ( Desai et al., 2025 ) learns binary codes of queries and keys, both with the model frozen. As the context grows, the indexer itself becomes the bottleneck ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Zan et al., 2026 ; Bai et al., 2026 ) . To reduce its cost, CSA ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026a ) , QSA ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) , and GLM-5.3-Flash SA ( Z.ai, 2026 ) compress every four keys into one before scoring them. HISA ( Xu et al., 2026 ) and LongCat LSA ( Zan et al., 2026 ) score blocks first and then only the keys inside the selected blocks. IndexCache ( Bai et al., 2026 ) , LongCat LSA and DeepSeek-V4.1 ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026b ) reuse the selection of one layer in the following layers. Each improvement divides the cost of the indexer by a constant, and its work per query therefore still grows linearly with the context. NSA ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) and MoBA ( Lu et al., 2025 ) instead pre-train the model with sparse attention from scratch, such that the indexer learns from the NTP loss alone. NSA scores each block by a learned compressed key, and MoBA by the mean of its keys. InfLLM-V2 ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) and SSA ( Mao et al., 2026a ) bring such block selection to existing dense models by fine-tuning. HSA ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026a ) and HSA-UltraLong ( Hu et al., 2026b ) also weight the output of each block by its score, such that the loss trains the scores directly. All of these methods still scan every block. PISA ( Tang et al., 2026 ) replaces this scan with a tree, but evaluates accuracy only at small scale (up to 16k tokens). At the other end, Quest ( Tang et al., 2024 ) , InfLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024a ) and MInference ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) select blocks based on simple summaries of their keys without any training. HiP ( Lee et al., 2025a ) searches the blocks with a tree, and its successor InfiniteHiP ( Lee et al., 2025b ) with three fixed stages. BLASST ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) instead skips blocks directly inside the attention kernel, without a dedicated indexer. Most of these methods summarise blocks of consecutive keys, which may hide a single relevant key ( Xiao et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2026a ) . Closest to LSA are methods that organise the keys by semantic content rather than by position. A few early works train at short context, with Reformer ( Kitaev et al., 2020 ) hashing keys into buckets, Routing Transformer ( Roy et al., 2021 ) learning k-means centroids, and Treeformer ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) routing each query down a learned tree. Most other works here only operate at inference time: ClusterKV ( Liu et al., 2025b ) and RetroInfer ( Chen et al., 2026 ) cluster the keys during prefill and score every centroid at decode (flat search), Squeezed Attention ( Hooper et al., 2025b ) , Multipole Attention ( Hooper et al., 2025a ) and LycheeCluster ( Li et al., 2026 ) search two levels (fixed search), and IceCache ( Mao et al., 2026b ) descends a tree of keys (tree search), while RetrievalAttention ( Liu et al., 2025a ) links the keys in a nearest-neighbour graph. All of these inference methods are training-free, only Squeezed Attention speeds up prefill, and only partially, and none are evaluated at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens). Figure 3: D-LSA design. Left: D-LSA (Flat). Indexer keys: 1 projection and L2 norm, 2 pooling (4:1), 3 bottom-up agglomerative clustering (Ward’s method), 4 bucket cache (centroids and index table). Indexer queries: A sum over query heads, projection and L2 norm, B scoring the cached centroids and selecting the top-p buckets per query, C expanding the buckets into indices (sink + top-k long-range + window), D attention over those indices (one index list per query shared by all query heads). Right: D-LSA (Tree) groups the buckets into a hierarchy of clusters, a query descends using beam search (close in the latent space but scattered through the KV cache). 3 Latent Sparse Attention (LSA) LSA is a sparse attention layer for ultra-long context. It clusters keys by content, in a space that is learned: through index projections in D-LSA, and through the attention’s own keys in N-LSA. LSA can replace the attention of a pre-trained layer by distillation (D-LSA) or be trained natively with the model (N-LSA). In both settings, the indices for the attention are selected from the keys and queries by the same process. We first describe this process, numbered as in Figure 3 , which consists of semantic clustering of the index keys k j ( idx ) k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})} , and the search with the index queries q i ( idx ) q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} so that each query selects its keys. We then describe the specifics of D-LSA and N-LSA. 3.1 Semantic Clustering 1 Key normalisation. Each index key k j ( idx ) k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})} is first L2 normalised: k j ( idx ) ← k j ( idx ) ∥ k j ( idx ) ∥ k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\leftarrow\frac{k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}}{\lVert k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\rVert} 2 Pooling. Consecutive keys are then compressed, as in CSA ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026a ) , QSA ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) and GLM-5.3-Flash SA ( Z.ai, 2026 ) , to improve computational efficiency. Here, every n pool n_{\mathrm{pool}} consecutive index keys are summed into one pool key k pool ( idx ) k_{\mathrm{pool}}^{(\mathrm{idx})} , so that clustering runs over T / n pool T/n_{\mathrm{pool}} pool keys rather than T T keys. 3 Clustering. Keys are clustered in cluster blocks of n cluster n_{\mathrm{cluster}} consecutive keys. Once a cluster block contains all its keys, its pool keys are clustered bottom up with Ward’s method ( Ward, 1963 ) into m m buckets (Algorithm 1 in Appendix B ). Each pool key starts as a bucket of its own, and each bucket keeps the sum of its keys, whose normalisation is its centroid c b c_{b} . In every round, all pairs of buckets that are each other’s cheapest merge are merged in parallel. The cost of a merge is how much it increases the keys’ total squared distance from their centroid (Ward’s criterion). Merging stops once there are m = n cluster / n ¯ b m=n_{\mathrm{cluster}}/\bar{n}_{b} buckets, where n ¯ b \bar{n}_{b} is the average number of keys per bucket, such that every cluster block holds the same number of buckets. A merge is skipped if the merged bucket would hold more than n b max n_{b}^{\mathrm{max}} keys. 4 Bucket cache. The bucket cache B cache ( idx ) B_{\mathrm{cache}}^{(\mathrm{idx})} stores the centroid c b c_{b} of every bucket and an index table of the positions of its keys. This is so later selected buckets can ‘expand’ into their key indices. With one centroid per n ¯ b \bar{n}_{b} keys, it corresponds to a small fraction of the KV cache. Once a cluster block is clustered, its buckets never change. In the Tree variant, this clustering process is repeated to group the buckets into multiple levels of a hierarchy. 3.2 Semantic Search We now describe how the top- k k key indices are extracted for each query, and then submitted to attention. We first describe the process for Flat , in which there is only one level of buckets, and then discuss Tree . A Query normalisation. Each index query q i ( idx ) q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} is first L2 normalised: q i ( idx ) ← q i ( idx ) ∥ q i ( idx ) ∥ q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\leftarrow\frac{q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}}{\lVert q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}\rVert} B Scoring. The index query scores the unit-norm centroid of every bucket in the cluster blocks before its own via s i , b = c b ⋅ q i ( idx ) s_{i,b}=c_{b}\cdot q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})} , which compares buckets of any size on one scale, and selects the top- p p buckets. Its own cluster block is not clustered yet, and its keys are covered by the window instead. C Expansion. The selected p p buckets are expanded into their keys, best first, until k k ‘long-range’ keys are selected. As every bucket holds at least n pool n_{\mathrm{pool}} keys, p p is chosen such that p ⋅ n pool ≥ k p\cdot n_{\mathrm{pool}}\geq k , and so expansion always fills k k keys. Besides the k k long-range keys, every query attends to n sink n_{\mathrm{sink}} sink keys ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) and the n w n_{w} most recent keys (window). A key of a selected bucket that falls in the sink or the window is already attended to, and the expansion moves on to the next key instead. We set the window to one cluster block, n w = n cluster n_{w}=n_{\mathrm{cluster}} , so that the window covers every key not yet clustered. This gives each query i i a set J i J_{i} of at most n sink + k + n w n_{\mathrm{sink}}+k+n_{w} key indices. D Attention. Attention is then computed only over the keys indexed by J i J_{i} . Abstract Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-Flash ( Qwen-3.8-27B ) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7 × 22.7\times ( 72.4 × 72.4\times ) in prefill and 4.6 × 4.6\times ( 42.5 × 42.5\times ) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6 × 1.6\times per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context. 1 Introduction Figure 1: D-LSA and N-LSA overview. Top: one attention layer. The keys are pooled and clustered into buckets. A query ( ) scores the bucket centroids ( ) and attends only to the selected long-range keys (plus sink and window). Bottom: accuracy and performance (P: prefill, D: decode, T: training) for both D-LSA and N-LSA. D-LSA is shown with flat search. Its subquadratic variant, D-LSA (Tree), follows a similar trend (Figure 5 ). Large language models have moved from answering single requests to agentic workflows in long-horizon tasks, such as software engineering and open-ended scientific research ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . These tasks keep growing in length ( Kwa et al., 2025 ) , and models with longer context windows tend to score higher on them ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) . In line with this trend, recent models extend their context windows to 1M tokens and beyond ( Gemini Team, 2024 ; MiniMax, 2025 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026a ; Qwen Team, 2026a ) . At this context size, attention dominates the cost, as its work grows with context ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Dao et al., 2022 ) . An established technique to reduce such costs is sparse attention ( Hoefler et al., 2021 ) , in which each query attends to only a subset of the keys, chosen by a fixed pattern ( Child et al., 2019 ; Beltagy et al., 2020 ; Zaheer et al., 2020 ) , by their content ( Kitaev et al., 2020 ; Roy et al., 2021 ) , or by a dedicated indexer ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Recent frontier models are increasingly adopting sparse attention, in which keys are selected using a dedicated indexer ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Qwen Team, 2026a ) . However, current indexers still score every preceding key, or block of keys, for each query. This remains expensive (quadratic in prefill, linear in decode), and becomes a bottleneck at long context ( Zan et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . For example, at 10M tokens, 98% of the prefill time of a sparse attention layer is spent on indexing (Figure 2 ). The cost of sparse attention at ultra-long context is therefore dominated by the cost of finding the keys. To address this, we introduce Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), which clusters keys in a learned latent space and lets each query search the clusters instead of scoring every key. This can be done using only one level of clustering ( Flat ), or with a hierarchy of clusters ( Tree ), which makes the prefill subquadratic. Furthermore, we propose two trainable designs: D-LSA, which adds LSA to pre-trained models and only trains small projection matrices per layer (contribution #1) , and N-LSA, which trains LSA natively with the Next-Token Prediction (NTP) loss alone (contribution #2) . We evaluate state-of-the-art models ( Qwen-3.8-27B and GLM-5.3-Flash ) beyond their advertised context, up to 10M tokens (contribution #3) , on RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) , which is an established long-context benchmark, and PaperTrail, which we developed to test long-context scientific understanding by finding and connecting facts across unseen scientific papers (contribution #4) . Finally, we integrate LSA into SGLang ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) 1 1 1 github.com/Prefrontal-AI/sglang with context parallelism, provide GPU kernels for H200 and B300, and release the code 2 2 2 github.com/Prefrontal-AI/latent-sparse-attention with all training and inference details (contribution #5) . Figure 1 outlines our contributions. 2 Sparse Attention In full attention, every query attends to every preceding key. Prefilling a context of T T tokens therefore costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( T 2 ) \mathcal{O}(T^{2}) , and decoding one token costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(T) . In sparse attention, the work is split between an indexer and the attention. For each query, the indexer selects which keys the attention attends to 3 3 3 In this view, full attention corresponds to an indexer that returns the indices of all preceding keys. . With a fixed budget of k k keys, the attention then costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ k ) \mathcal{O}(Tk) to prefill and 𝒪 ⁡ ( k ) \mathcal{O}(k) per decoded token. If the indexer selects the most relevant keys, this is sufficient to stay close to the accuracy of full attention (Appendix A ). However, the indexer has a cost. Since it must score all preceding keys, it typically remains 𝒪 ⁡ ( T 2 ) \mathcal{O}(T^{2}) in prefill and 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(T) in decode, though with reduced constant factors. This makes ultra-long context still prohibitively expensive. For example, at 10M tokens the indexer takes 98% of the prefill time of traditional sparse attention (Figure 2 ), and a ‘free’ indexer would make sparse attention a further 58 × 58\times faster in prefill and 8.9 × 8.9\times in decode. Speedup of sparse attention over full attention ( blue ), share of the indexer ( % ), and potential speedup over sparse attention if the indexer were ‘free’ ( green ). 2.1 Design Choices Sparse attention methods can be categorised by their indexer designs and how they are trained. Token Sparse Attention. For each query, a lightweight indexer (fewer heads, smaller dimension, lower precision) scores every preceding key and selects which to attend to. Block Sparse Attention. Consecutive keys are grouped into blocks, and each query scores blocks instead of every key. All keys of the selected blocks are sent to the attention. Semantic Sparse Attention. Keys are clustered by similarity rather than position, and each query scores one centroid per cluster. All keys of the selected clusters are sent to the attention. For the last two categories, a query can search the groups in three ways. Flat search scores every group directly, which is 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(T) work per query. Fixed search adds a shallow hierarchy and refines from coarse to fine groups, which is also 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(T) per query. Tree search descends a deeper hierarchy and expands only the groups it keeps at each level, which is 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) \mathcal{O}(\log T) per query. An indexer can be training-free, distilled from a pre-trained model, or trained natively on the NTP loss alone. 2.2 Related Work Table 1: Sparse attention methods compared. We focus on methods that keep the whole KV cache and select keys per query, unlike fixed sparse patterns ( Child et al., 2019 ; Beltagy et al., 2020 ; Zaheer et al., 2020 ) and KV cache eviction techniques ( Zhang et al., 2023b ; Li et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2024b ) . Among distillation methods, DSA ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) and MiniMax SA ( Lai et al., 2026 ) first distil the indexer and then continue training the full model under sparse attention. Alternatively, SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) distils a gate over pooled blocks and HashAttention ( Desai et al., 2025 ) learns binary codes of queries and keys, both with the model frozen. As the context grows, the indexer itself becomes the bottleneck ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Zan et al., 2026 ; Bai et al., 2026 ) . To reduce its cost, CSA ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026a ) , QSA ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) , and GLM-5.3-Flash SA ( Z.ai, 2026 ) compress every four keys into one before scoring them. HISA ( Xu et al., 2026 ) and LongCat LSA ( Zan et al., 2026 ) score blocks first and then only the keys inside the selected blocks. IndexCache ( Bai et al., 2026 ) , LongCat LSA and DeepSeek-V4.1 ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026b ) reuse the selection of one layer in the following layers. Each improvement divides the cost of the indexer by a constant, and its work per query therefore still grows linearly with the context. NSA ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) and MoBA ( Lu et al., 2025 ) instead pre-train the model with sparse attention from scratch, such that the indexer learns from the NTP loss alone. NSA scores each block by a learned compressed key, and MoBA by the mean of its keys. InfLLM-V2 ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) and SSA ( Mao et al., 2026a ) bring such block selection to existing dense models by fine-tuning. HSA ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026a ) and HSA-UltraLong ( Hu et al., 2026b ) also weight the output of each block by its score, such that the loss trains the scores directly. All of these methods still scan every block. PISA ( Tang et al., 2026 ) replaces this scan with a tree, but evaluates accuracy only at small scale (up to 16k tokens). At the other end, Quest ( Tang et al., 2024 ) , InfLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024a ) and MInference ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) select blocks based on simple summaries of their keys without any training. HiP ( Lee et al., 2025a ) searches the blocks with a tree, and its successor InfiniteHiP ( Lee et al., 2025b ) with three fixed stages. BLASST ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) instead skips blocks directly inside the attention kernel, without a dedicated indexer. Most of these methods summarise blocks of consecutive keys, which may hide a single relevant key ( Xiao et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2026a ) . Closest to LSA are methods that organise the keys by semantic content rather than by position. A few early works train at short context, with Reformer ( Kitaev et al., 2020 ) hashing keys into buckets, Routing Transformer ( Roy et al., 2021 ) learning k-means centroids, and Treeformer ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) routing each query down a learned tree. All of these inference methods are training-free, only Squeezed Attention speeds up prefill, and only partially, and none are evaluated at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens). items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.42116 (cs) [Submitted on 30 Oct 2026] Title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer Authors: Yuzhe Liu , Haolin Tian , Tonghan Wang View a PDF of the paper titled ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer, by Yuzhe Liu and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget. items.content: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer Yuzhe Liu † † thanks: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China Haolin Tian 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China Tonghan Wang Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China Affiliation: Correspondence to: thw@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn Abstract In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model’s original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of ∼ \sim 19K tokens, ACCT’s KV conversion achieves a 6.5 6.5 – 21.2 × 21.2\times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) systems are evolving from serving a single model to heterogeneous deployments comprising models of different scales and capabilities ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Such systems may dynamically route requests according to task difficulty, latency requirements, and resource availability ( Ong et al., 2025 ) . Meanwhile, conversation histories, retrieved documents, and task states often persist across requests, far outliving any individual model invocation ( Packer et al., 2023 ; Gim et al., 2024 ) . Thus, while the executing model may change, the context often remains the same. Yet when the same context is handed to a new target model, the target typically must process the entire context again to construct the internal states required for inference. As contexts grow and are used more frequently across models, the costs of repeated computation and state construction accumulate. Enabling models to reuse context computation performed by another model, is therefore an important challenge for efficient heterogeneous LLM systems. Standard caching mechanisms reduce repeated computation within a model but do not directly make its KV cache reusable by other models. KV caching reuses states for preceding tokens during generations, while prefix caching extends this reuse across requests served by the same model ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ) . These states, however, depend jointly on the model’s parameters and architectures and are generally not interchangeable across models, even when the models belong to the same family ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) . Allowing a target model to build on context computation already performed by a source model requires transforming source KV into KV that the target can read directly. The transfer process should organize information around the target’s reasoning needs, retaining content relevant to the current query under a specified budget, and making it accessible by the target. To this end, we propose Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer (ACCT) for reusing context computation between models of different scales within the same family. ACCT transfers KV already produced by the source to sparse KV that the target can consume directly. To reuse source context computation under a limited KV capacity, ACCT achieves information selection for the target, KV budget allocation, and target KV generation through three lightweight components. The Cartographer uses source context and query representations to rank content tokens for every target layer and KV head. The Allocator assigns capacity across layers and heads under a global budget; together with the content token rankings, it determines which KV is retained. The Compiler converts selected source KV into KV for the corresponding target layers and KV heads. After mounting the transferred KV, the target reads context information through its own attention mechanism, without re-encoding the raw context, and performs only query encoding and subsequent autoregressive generation. This interface integrates context computation already performed by the source into the target’s regular inference process, allowing context encoding and downstream reasoning to be carried out by different models. ACCT aims to preserve the target’s reasoning capabilities while avoiding its re-encoding of the raw context. We evaluate ACCT on five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks across six directed model pairs. Using Target Full , in which the target model processes the complete context, as the reference, ACCT closely matches its performance on many tasks and surpasses it on some. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT’s KV conversion achieves a 6.5 6.5 – 21.2 × 21.2\times speedup over target context prefill. These results show that a target can use context information through transferred KV to support subsequent reasoning even without seeing the raw context itself. ACCT thus demonstrates the feasibility of treating context computation as a resource that can be reused across models, opening new possibilities for independently organizing context processing and reasoning in heterogeneous model systems. 2 Related Work Heterogeneous LLM Serving. FrugalGPT ( Chen et al., 2024 ) constructs model cascades to reduce inference costs, while RouteLLM ( Ong et al., 2025 ) learns routing policies between models with different capabilities and costs. These approaches focus on selecting the executing model; ACCT complements them by enabling reuse of previously computed context representations when execution switches to a different-scale model. Context Reuse in LLM Inference. Prompt Cache ( Gim et al., 2024 ) reuses attention states across requests, while H 2 O ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , SnapKV ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and PyramidKV ( Cai et al., 2024 ) reduce retained KV states through token selection or layer-wise budgeting. These methods reuse or compress states within the model that produced them. Extending reuse across models, DroidSpeak ( Liu et al., 2024 ) shares caches between same-architecture variants of a common base model and recomputes critical context layers in the receiver. ACCT instead converts representations across model scales without target-side context recomputation. Beyond computational reuse, C2C ( Fu et al., 2025 ) supports semantic communication across model sizes and families by projecting and fusing source KV with the receiver’s own context KV, avoiding intermediate text generation. Its full method retains receiver-side context encoding, whereas ACCT constructs the target’s context memory from source representations under a global state budget and runs the target only on the query and subsequent generation. Accordingly, neither method in its original formulation provides a matched baseline for our setting, which requires cross-scale context-state transfer without target-side context encoding. 3 Methods ACCT converts context representations already computed by a source model into sparse target KV, allowing the target model to answer queries without re-encoding the full context. Figure 1: ACCT combines Cartographer selection, Allocator budgeting, and Compiler conversion to transfer source KV into sparse target KV for inference without context re-encoding. 3.1 Transfer objective and overall workflow Consider frozen source and target models F S , F T F_{S},F_{T} from the same model family, with a context c c containing N N tokens and a query q q containing Q Q tokens. The source model processes the concatenated context and query to obtain final-layer context and query hidden states H c , H q H_{c},H_{q} , selected intermediate-layer context states { H c ( r ) } r ∈ ℛ \{H_{c}^{(r)}\}_{r\in\mathcal{R}} , and context KV. ℛ \mathcal{R} indexes the selected source intermediate layers. The target has L T L_{T} layers and H T H_{T} KV heads per layer, each storing d T d_{T} -dimensional keys and values. We call KV head h h in layer ℓ \ell a target unit p = ( ℓ , h ) p=(\ell,h) , giving P = L T ​ H T P=L_{T}H_{T} units. We collectively call the three modules that convert source representations into sparse target KV the transfer interface: Cartographer scores context tokens for each unit using context and query information; Allocator assigns retention capacities under a global budget (the total number of tokens allowed across all target units) and selects by score; Compiler converts only selected source representations into target-readable keys and values. The budget counts retained context tokens across physical KV heads; in grouped-query attention, query heads sharing one KV head are not counted separately. Let I p I_{p} be the set of original indices retained by unit p p , i i an index in this set, and K ^ p , i , V ^ p , i \widehat{K}_{p,i},\widehat{V}_{p,i} the corresponding Compiler outputs. Denote the transferred context cache constructed from c , q c,q for the target by 𝒞 ^ S → T ​ ( c , q ) \widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{S\to T}(c,q) , where S → T S\to T indicates source-to-target transfer: 𝒞 ^ S → T ​ ( c , q ) = { { ( i , K ^ p , i , V ^ p , i ) : i ∈ I p } } p = 1 P . \widehat{\mathcal{C}}_{S\to T}(c,q)=\left\{\left\{(i,\widehat{K}_{p,i},\widehat{V}_{p,i}):i\in I_{p}\right\}\right\}_{p=1}^{P}. (1) The cache preserves original token indices for positional encoding. After loading these KV pairs, the target only processes the query and generates the answer. 3.2 Constructing sparse target KV from source representations 3.2.1 Cartographer: scoring context tokens for each KV head Different target units serve different roles, so a token may differ in importance across units; its importance also depends on the query and its context position. Cartographer therefore combines source hidden states H c , H q H_{c},H_{q} , target layer and KV-head information, and token position to score context token i i in unit p p as S p , i S_{p,i} , establishing retention priorities within each unit. Specifically, S p , i = f o ​ ( γ p ⊙ x i + β p + W m ​ m p , i + W ϕ ​ ϕ i ) . S_{p,i}=f_{o}(\gamma_{p}\odot x_{i}+\beta_{p}+W_{m}m_{p,i}+W_{\phi}\phi_{i}). (2) Cartographer first extracts query-relevant content shared across units to avoid repeated query–context interaction. x i x_{i} is a token vector extracted and projected from H c H_{c} . γ p , β p \gamma_{p},\beta_{p} are scaling and shifting vectors derived from the unit and query-relevant content. m p , i m_{p,i} computes matching scores between token i i and that content conditioned on identification features of the target layer and KV head. The two-dimensional vector ϕ i \phi_{i} records token i i ’s normalized position in the context and its normalized log-distance from the context end. Learned matrices W m , W ϕ W_{m},W_{\phi} project matching and positional features to the token-vector dimension, f o f_{o} maps the combined vector to a scalar, and ⊙ \odot denotes elementwise multiplication. Feature computations and the shared architecture are detailed in Appendix A.1. 3.2.2 Allocator: assigning per-head capacities under a fixed budget Target units may need different amounts of context, which uniform allocation under a fixed budget cannot accommodate. Allocator therefore learns a capacity for each unit, a trainable parameter controlling its retention count, and determines the retained tokens based on Cartographer’s ranking. To prevent context immediately preceding the query from being entirely discarded by ranking or capacity competition, each unit reserves the final τ \tau context tokens and allocates the remaining capacity to earlier context, and the prefix contains N − τ N-\tau tokens. Given retention ratio ρ \rho , the budget allows an average of k = max ⁡ ( τ , ⌈ ρ ​ N ⌉ ) k=\max(\tau,\lceil\rho N\rceil) context tokens per target unit, including the reserved tail. ⌈ ⋅ ⌉ \lceil\cdot\rceil rounds upward. Subtracting the reserved P ​ τ P\tau from total capacity P ​ k Pk leaves a global budget of P ⁡ ( k − τ ) P(k-\tau) for the prefix. Allocation must respect both prefix length and the total budget. Let α p \alpha_{p} be unit p p ’s learned capacity and b p b_{p} its real-valued prefix capacity before rounding. The function σ ⁡ ( x ) = 1 / ( 1 + e − x ) \sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x}) bounds the capacity fraction between zero and one, while a shared adjustment λ \lambda enforces the total budget: b p = ( N − τ ) ​ σ ​ ( α p − λ ) , ∑ p = 1 P b p = P ⁡ ( k − τ ) . b_{p}=(N-\tau)\sigma(\alpha_{p}-\lambda),\qquad\sum_{p=1}^{P}b_{p}=P(k-\tau). (3) After converting b p b_{p} to integer prefix capacities k p k_{p} while preserving the total budget, each unit selects its k p k_{p} highest-scoring prefix tokens and adds the final τ \tau tokens to form I p I_{p} , retaining k p + τ k_{p}+\tau tokens in total. Answer prediction supervises the learning of α p \alpha_{p} (Section 3.3). Allocation details are in Appendix C. 3.2.3 Compiler: converting selected source representations into target KV The retained set I p I_{p} determines which context tokens supply KV to target unit p p , but their source KV cannot be used directly by the target model. Compiler therefore converts selected source KV into target KV, using final-layer states H c H_{c} and three selected intermediate-layer states { H c ( r ) } r ∈ ℛ \{H_{c}^{(r)}\}_{r\in\mathcal{R}} for context-dependent corrections. For each target unit, Bridge applies a linear transformation with bias to the selected tokens’ source KV from a predetermined source layer and KV head, producing K p , i B , V p , i B K^{B}_{p,i},V^{B}_{p,i} . A correction network predicts context-dependent corrections Δ ​ K p , i , Δ ​ V p , i \Delta K_{p,i},\Delta V_{p,i} based on the context. Adding them gives the result: K ^ p , i = K p , i B + Δ ​ K p , i , V ^ p , i = V p , i B + Δ ​ V p , i . \widehat{K}_{p,i}=K^{B}_{p,i}+\Delta K_{p,i},\qquad\widehat{V}_{p,i}=V^{B}_{p,i}+\Delta V_{p,i}. (4) The correction network reads the final-layer source states H c H_{c} and the three selected intermediate-layer state sequences { H c ( r ) } r ∈ ℛ \{H_{c}^{(r)}\}_{r\in\mathcal{R}} , sharing the context computation and each selected token’s representation across target units: ( Δ ​ K p , i , Δ ​ V p , i ) = Correction ψ ⁡ ( H c , { H c ( r ) } r ∈ ℛ , δ p , i , p ) . (\Delta K_{p,i},\Delta V_{p,i})=\operatorname{Correction}_{\psi}\!\left(H_{c},\{H_{c}^{(r)}\}_{r\in\mathcal{R}},\delta_{p},i;\,p\right). (5) Here, δ p = | I p | / N \delta_{p}=|I_{p}|/N is the retained fraction, ψ \psi is trainable parameters. Source-layer/head correspondence, the correction architecture, positional-encoding handling, and fitting details are in Appendix A.2. 3.3 The Training Scheme We train the three components in stages. We first learn scoring and allocation with target-native KV, which is keys and values produced by the target itself when encoding context. We then fix the retained token sets and train Compiler to convert the selected source representations into the corresponding target KV. Only the transfer interface is updated in these stages, leaving the source and the target model intact. Scoring: learn to rank by the effect of token removal. To retain useful tokens, our supervision reflects the effect of discarding them. We remove a context token’s key and value while keeping the target model’s query vectors and the remaining keys and values fixed, then renormalize the remaining attention weights. A larger change in the attention output indicates a more important token. We collect this change at the query end and on subsequent tokens generated by the target for supervision, aggregating it per KV head as deletion utility u p , i u_{p,i} . To train Cartographer before learning the Allocator, we temporarily assign equal retention capacity to every target unit. Within each unit, we rank prefix tokens by deletion utility; the boundary between the last retained token and the first discarded token defines the retention cutoff. Tokens on opposite sides of the retention cutoff often have similar deletion utilities, making them the hardest cases for the Cartographer to distinguish. We therefore sample training pairs near the retention cutoff. Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China Haolin Tian 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China Tonghan Wang Affiliation: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China Affiliation: Correspondence to: thw@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn Abstract In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model’s original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of ∼ \sim 19K tokens, ACCT’s KV conversion achieves a 6.5 6.5 – 21.2 × 21.2\times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) systems are evolving from serving a single model to heterogeneous deployments comprising models of different scales and capabilities ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Such systems may dynamically route requests according to task difficulty, latency requirements, and resource availability ( Ong et al., 2025 ) . Meanwhile, conversation histories, retrieved documents, and task states often persist across requests, far outliving any individual model invocation ( Packer et al., 2023 ; Gim et al., 2024 ) . Thus, while the executing model may change, the context often remains the same. Yet when the same context is handed to a new target model, the target typically must process the entire context again to construct the internal states required for inference. As contexts grow and are used more frequently across models, the costs of repeated computation and state construction accumulate. Enabling models to reuse context computation performed by another model, is therefore an important challenge for efficient heterogeneous LLM systems. Standard caching mechanisms reduce repeated computation within a model but do not directly make its KV cache reusable by other models. KV caching reuses states for preceding tokens during generations, while prefix caching extends this reuse across requests served by the same model ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ) . These states, however, depend jointly on the model’s parameters and architectures and are generally not interchangeable across models, even when the models belong to the same family ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) . Allowing a target model to build on context computation already performed by a source model requires transforming source KV into KV that the target can read directly. The transfer process should organize information around the target’s reasoning needs, retaining content relevant to the current query under a specified budget, and making it accessible by the target. To this end, we propose Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer (ACCT) for reusing context computation between models of different scales within the same family. ACCT transfers KV already produced by the source to sparse KV that the target can consume directly. To reuse source context computation under a limited KV capacity, ACCT achieves information selection for the target, KV budget allocation, and target KV generation through three lightweight components. The Cartographer uses source context and query representations to rank content tokens for every target layer and KV head. The Allocator assigns capacity across layers and heads under a global budget; together with the content token rankings, it determines which KV is retained. The Compiler converts selected source KV into KV for the corresponding target layers and KV heads. After mounting the transferred KV, the target reads context information through its own attention mechanism, without re-encoding the raw context, and performs only query encoding and subsequent autoregressive generation. This interface integrates context computation already performed by the source into the target’s regular inference process, allowing context encoding and downstream reasoning to be carried out by different models. ACCT aims to preserve the target’s reasoning capabilities while avoiding its re-encoding of the raw context. We evaluate ACCT on five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks across six directed model pairs. Using Target Full , in which the target model processes the complete context, as the reference, ACCT closely matches its performance on many tasks and surpasses it on some. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT’s KV conversion achieves a 6.5 6.5 – 21.2 × 21.2\times speedup over target context prefill. These results show that a target can use context information through transferred KV to support subsequent reasoning even without seeing the raw context itself. ACCT thus demonstrates the feasibility of treating context computation as a resource that can be reused across models, opening new possibilities for independently organizing context processing and reasoning in heterogeneous model systems. 2 Related Work Heterogeneous LLM Serving. FrugalGPT ( Chen et al., 2024 ) constructs model cascades to reduce inference costs, while RouteLLM ( Ong et al., 2025 ) learns routing policies between models with different capabilities and costs. These approaches focus on selecting the executing model; ACCT complements them by enabling reuse of previously computed context representations when execution switches to a different-scale model. Context Reuse in LLM Inference. Prompt Cache ( Gim et al., 2024 ) reuses attention states across requests, while H 2 O ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , SnapKV ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and PyramidKV ( Cai et al., 2024 ) reduce retained KV states through token selection or layer-wise budgeting. These methods reuse or compress states within the model that produced them. Extending reuse across models, DroidSpeak ( Liu et al., 2024 ) shares caches between same-architecture variants of a common base model and recomputes critical context layers in the receiver. ACCT instead converts representations across model scales without target-side context recomputation. Beyond computational reuse, C2C ( Fu et al., 2025 ) supports semantic communication across model sizes and families by projecting and fusing source KV with the receiver’s own context KV, avoiding intermediate text generation. Its full method retains receiver-side context encoding, whereas ACCT constructs the target’s context memory from source representations under a global state budget and runs the target only on the query and subsequent generation.
