items.content: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models Juntao Cheng Affiliation: UIUC Jinzhou Tang Affiliation: UCSD Fan Feng Affiliation: UCSD Henrik I. Christensen Affiliation: UCSD Yujia Zheng Affiliation: UIUC Abstract World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success. 1 Introduction The action a robot performs when stacking a single block atop another depends on the position of both blocks and the fact that the gripper is currently holding the uppermost block. The camera image’s pixels will change significantly if the robot removes the tablecloth or clears away the clutter located behind the table; however, this will have no effect upon the motion itself. WAMs (World Action Models) like Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , and Cosmos 3 ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) are able to extract latent variables from images and can be used to generate actions from those latent variables, while also being capable of generating images of potential subsequent frames. Since prediction has to account for the whole scene, these latent variables also describe the tablecloth and the clutter. We refer to the latent variables that cause the demonstrated actions as action-relevant latent variables, and to the others as nuisance variables. Fitting the demonstrations well does not in itself guarantee that the WAM is acting from the action-relevant latent variables. For each step of the demonstration we could write o t = f ⁡ ( s t ) o_{t}=f(s_{t}) and a t = π ⁡ ( s t , η t ) a_{t}=\pi(s_{t},\eta_{t}) where s t s_{t} is the latent state, f f is some unknown invertible function, π \pi is some unknown action mechanism and η t \eta_{t} is exogenous noise. Separating action from prediction is then about recovering (up to certain indeterminacies) the action-relevant latent variables and which of those variables cause each action dimension. Without further assumptions, the latent causal variables cannot be identified from their observations ( Hyvärinen and Pajunen, 1999 ; Locatello et al., 2019 ) . Observing the actions as well doesn’t help with this ambiguity, as two models can give rise to the same distribution of ( o t , a t ) (o_{t},a_{t}) whilst their latent variables differ by an arbitrary invertible transformation. This transformation can mix the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance ones, so a very flexible action head could generate actions from variables which also contain information about the tablecloth (which doesn’t in fact cause the motion) and still fit the demonstrations equally well. To make latent variables identifiable, existing works in nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) introduce auxiliary variables, such as domain or time indices, or exploit temporal dependence ( Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2016 ; Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2017 ; Hyvärinen et al., 2019 ; Khemakhem et al., 2020 ) . For latent causal processes, identifiability has been established under sufficient temporal dependence ( Yao et al., 2022 ) and conditions on the latent dynamics ( Song et al., 2023 ) . Interventions with known targets have also been introduced to pin down the latents ( Lippe et al., 2022 ) . Many of these assumptions might be violated for demonstrations in complex real-world scenarios such as robotics, where some time steps might be independent, the latent dynamics might not be Markov, and controlled interventions are either prohibitively expensive or simply impossible. Another line of research constrains the generative process by restricting the function class or enforcing sparsity in the dependency structure ( Kivva et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2022 ; Lachapelle et al., 2022 ) . Most of these studies, similar to those previously discussed, aim to recover all latent variables, requiring their conditions to hold even for nuisance variables that a robot can disregard. In contrast, results on partial identifiability focus on a subset of latent variables, determined by side information accompanying the data, such as content shared across views ( von Kügelgen et al., 2021 ; Yao et al., 2024 ) , components invariant across domains ( Kong et al., 2022 ) , or elements relevant to specific tasks ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . For robots learning from demonstrations, the relevant subset consists of the latent causes underlying the demonstrated actions. Since no view, domain, or task label directly specifies this subset, the actions themselves must indicate which latent variables are pertinent. This raises the following question: From demonstrations alone, can we separate what causes actions from what prediction needs? In this work, we answer this question with a constraint on the action side that leaves prediction free to use every latent variable. Since each action is generated from only part of the latent state, constraining the number of dependencies between latent variables and action dimensions can separate that part from the rest. Specifically, we prove that, without such a constraint and under nondegeneracy conditions, fitting the demonstrations only ensures that each action dimension of the estimated mechanism depends on at least as many latent variables as the true one (Prop. 1 ). We then incorporate a sparsity regularization on the dependency structure between latent state and action variables during estimation. Under the same conditions, the lower bound becomes an equality and the dependency structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables (Thm. 1 ). Moreover, we prove that the estimated action-relevant variables under the proposed constraint are an invertible function of the ground-truth latent variables causing the true action (Thm. 2 ). The latent causes of the actions are thus identified as a block and are separated from the nuisance variables. The theoretical guarantee relies purely on observational demonstrations, without requiring any interventions, sufficient temporal dependence, or any assumptions about the latent dynamics. The framework also allows dependence between action-relevant latent variables and the nuisance variables (e.g., a tablecloth could be correlated with the positions of the cubes). According to the established theory, we propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which adds a sparse routing path from the visual and task tokens to the action head in Cosmos 3 and applies a token-level surrogate of the constraint to this path (Sec. 4 ). In synthetic scenarios, we validate the identifiability claims shown by our theory. On RoboCasa365, LIBERO, and a real Franka R3 robot, the routing path improves aggregate closed-loop success over Cosmos 3 without it, and in most visualized frames its routing mass falls on the object being moved and its target (Sec. 5 ). 2 Problem setup Data. Demonstration data are sequences { o t , a t } t = 1 T \{o_{t},a_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} with o t ∈ ℝ d o o_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{o}} and a t ∈ ℝ d a a_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} . Christensen Affiliation: UCSD Yujia Zheng Affiliation: UIUC Abstract World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success. 1 Introduction The action a robot performs when stacking a single block atop another depends on the position of both blocks and the fact that the gripper is currently holding the uppermost block. The camera image’s pixels will change significantly if the robot removes the tablecloth or clears away the clutter located behind the table; however, this will have no effect upon the motion itself. WAMs (World Action Models) like Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , and Cosmos 3 ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) are able to extract latent variables from images and can be used to generate actions from those latent variables, while also being capable of generating images of potential subsequent frames. Since prediction has to account for the whole scene, these latent variables also describe the tablecloth and the clutter. We refer to the latent variables that cause the demonstrated actions as action-relevant latent variables, and to the others as nuisance variables. Fitting the demonstrations well does not in itself guarantee that the WAM is acting from the action-relevant latent variables. For each step of the demonstration we could write o t = f ⁡ ( s t ) o_{t}=f(s_{t}) and a t = π ⁡ ( s t , η t ) a_{t}=\pi(s_{t},\eta_{t}) where s t s_{t} is the latent state, f f is some unknown invertible function, π \pi is some unknown action mechanism and η t \eta_{t} is exogenous noise. Separating action from prediction is then about recovering (up to certain indeterminacies) the action-relevant latent variables and which of those variables cause each action dimension. Without further assumptions, the latent causal variables cannot be identified from their observations ( Hyvärinen and Pajunen, 1999 ; Locatello et al., 2019 ) . Observing the actions as well doesn’t help with this ambiguity, as two models can give rise to the same distribution of ( o t , a t ) (o_{t},a_{t}) whilst their latent variables differ by an arbitrary invertible transformation. This transformation can mix the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance ones, so a very flexible action head could generate actions from variables which also contain information about the tablecloth (which doesn’t in fact cause the motion) and still fit the demonstrations equally well. To make latent variables identifiable, existing works in nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) introduce auxiliary variables, such as domain or time indices, or exploit temporal dependence ( Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2016 ; Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2017 ; Hyvärinen et al., 2019 ; Khemakhem et al., 2020 ) . For latent causal processes, identifiability has been established under sufficient temporal dependence ( Yao et al., 2022 ) and conditions on the latent dynamics ( Song et al., 2023 ) . Interventions with known targets have also been introduced to pin down the latents ( Lippe et al., 2022 ) . Many of these assumptions might be violated for demonstrations in complex real-world scenarios such as robotics, where some time steps might be independent, the latent dynamics might not be Markov, and controlled interventions are either prohibitively expensive or simply impossible. Another line of research constrains the generative process by restricting the function class or enforcing sparsity in the dependency structure ( Kivva et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2022 ; Lachapelle et al., 2022 ) . Most of these studies, similar to those previously discussed, aim to recover all latent variables, requiring their conditions to hold even for nuisance variables that a robot can disregard. In contrast, results on partial identifiability focus on a subset of latent variables, determined by side information accompanying the data, such as content shared across views ( von Kügelgen et al., 2021 ; Yao et al., 2024 ) , components invariant across domains ( Kong et al., 2022 ) , or elements relevant to specific tasks ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . For robots learning from demonstrations, the relevant subset consists of the latent causes underlying the demonstrated actions. Since no view, domain, or task label directly specifies this subset, the actions themselves must indicate which latent variables are pertinent. This raises the following question: From demonstrations alone, can we separate what causes actions from what prediction needs? In this work, we answer this question with a constraint on the action side that leaves prediction free to use every latent variable. Since each action is generated from only part of the latent state, constraining the number of dependencies between latent variables and action dimensions can separate that part from the rest. Specifically, we prove that, without such a constraint and under nondegeneracy conditions, fitting the demonstrations only ensures that each action dimension of the estimated mechanism depends on at least as many latent variables as the true one (Prop. 1 ). We then incorporate a sparsity regularization on the dependency structure between latent state and action variables during estimation. Under the same conditions, the lower bound becomes an equality and the dependency structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables (Thm. 1 ). Moreover, we prove that the estimated action-relevant variables under the proposed constraint are an invertible function of the ground-truth latent variables causing the true action (Thm. 2 ). The latent causes of the actions are thus identified as a block and are separated from the nuisance variables. The theoretical guarantee relies purely on observational demonstrations, without requiring any interventions, sufficient temporal dependence, or any assumptions about the latent dynamics. The framework also allows dependence between action-relevant latent variables and the nuisance variables (e.g., a tablecloth could be correlated with the positions of the cubes). According to the established theory, we propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which adds a sparse routing path from the visual and task tokens to the action head in Cosmos 3 and applies a token-level surrogate of the constraint to this path (Sec. 4 ). In synthetic scenarios, we validate the identifiability claims shown by our theory. On RoboCasa365, LIBERO, and a real Franka R3 robot, the routing path improves aggregate closed-loop success over Cosmos 3 without it, and in most visualized frames its routing mass falls on the object being moved and its target (Sec. 5 ). 2 Problem setup Data. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.42066 (cs) [Submitted on 30 Oct 2026] Title: The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results Authors: Omer Asim Ozturk , Cihan Aydiner View a PDF of the paper titled The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results, by Omer Asim Ozturk and 1 other authors View PDF Abstract: AI answers require more than apparent correctness: reviewers need to inspect their recorded basis. We introduce the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open, implementation-neutral specification for inference records with versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit unknowns. SEDIM, the knowledge and evidence architecture of Nage AI OS, is a reference implementation. We reference KLM v0.3 (repository tag v0.3.0). Empirical material consists of separate internal experiments, not end-to-end validation. A historical platform-domain routing benchmark reports 137/150 classifications across 15 classes (91.3%; nominal 95% Wilson interval 85.7-94.9%); the numerator is recovered from a rounded summary, and historical example membership is unverified. A native-model weight-path configuration yielded 0/15 successful answers in a corrected two-source test. A capacity-growth comparison could not establish a reliable effect because of a defective legacy scorer and missing original outputs. Lexical and scoped diagnostics each yielded AUC 0.008 for silent-versus-contradicted examples, below the registered minimum of 0.65. Legacy packing lost gold-containing text in 118/221 selected cases; repaired packing retained it in 221/221. These measure text presence, not answer quality. Python and TypeScript verifiers reportedly agreed on six checks per synthetic fixture; a separate production disclosure was not accepted. Restoration, re-derivation, human-rubric support, boundary isolation, and bounded-response evaluations remain proposed. Findings are internal and author-reported; historical observations are distinguished from later reproductions. Evidence visibility does not establish correctness, causal reliance, security, or regulatory compliance. Independent replication and a complete public audit package remain future work. Comments: 47 pages, 1 figure, 14 tables. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.42039 (cs) [Submitted on 30 Oct 2026] Title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice Authors: Artin Yousefi , Aizierjiang Aiersilan , Lorien C Abroms , David A Broniatowski View a PDF of the paper titled Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice, by Artin Yousefi and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? We audit six widely deployed LLMs from four providers on smoking cessation, a domain with codified clini- cal guidance and substantial public-health stakes, by putting the same four cessation questions to twelve user personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise, and smoking history, for a total of 2,880 responses. What the models say depends on who appears to be asking. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points, and in five of six models a persona presenting health- care expertise received fewer facts than a persona presenting none. We then evaluate one deployable intervention: a short system prompt specifying a factual floor, the set of core med- ical facts every user should receive when they are relevant, while leaving tone, vocabulary, and framing free to adapt. The prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in both magnitude and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another. Two cautions frame these results. Equal mention rates are not always the correct clinical target, because prescription cessation pharmacother- apy is not recommended for minors, so a defensible factual floor must be age-aware rather than uniform. And because our personas vary on several attributes at once, we report scenario- level differences rather than isolated effects of age or expertise. We release all 2,880 responses and the analysis code. items.content: Data Center / Cloud Diagnose Distributed AI Workload Failures with NVIDIA Attribution Use this open-source tool to correlate workload-scoped logs, metrics, and scheduler state into a reproducible diagnosis on your own cluster. Nov 02, 2026 By Gargi Prasad , Jason Sewall , Aaron Blakeman , Ajay Hotchandani and Ashwin Poojary Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA Attribution correlates workload-scoped logs, metrics, telemetry, and scheduler state to produce a structured diagnosis with outcome, root cause, affected nodes, supporting symptoms, and an evidence trail. The system operates through two deployable components: the Attribution Service, which exposes a REST API for the core attribution engine, and the Attribution Blueprint, a Python reference orchestrator that connects cluster schedulers and telemetry sources to the Service. The Blueprint ships with execution-context connectors for Slurm , Kueue, and static inputs, plus log and metric connectors for Loki, local files, Kubernetes pod logs, and PromQL metrics. In production across NVIDIA AI infrastructure, the system analyzes millions of workloads weekly across hundreds of thousands of GPUs and has identified fabric failure patterns around specific host and switch ports. The attribution process follows four stages: scoping the workload, collecting observations, extracting and correlating events through deterministic rules, and returning a structured result with terminal state and attributed domain. A worked example demonstrates how an NVLink signal integrity issue on one node is identified as the root cause while downstream NCCL errors across ranks are preserved as supporting symptoms. Next Steps Clone the NVIDIA Attribution repository to access the source code and sample workloads. Follow the quickstart to run the sample workflow and inspect diagnoses in the local dashboard. Review the Blueprint configuration reference to connect your own scheduler and telemetry backends. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more In distributed AI workloads, a single error can produce a cascade of symptoms. A GPU or fabric event may surface as NCCL errors on other ranks, scheduler state changes, and thousands of downstream messages. The reported exception shows where the workload stopped, not where the failure began. In this post, you’ll learn how to run NVIDIA Attribution on sample workload evidence, inspect the diagnosis, and explore how attribution rules identify failure patterns. NVIDIA Attribution correlates workload-scoped logs, metrics, telemetry, and scheduler state and returns a structured diagnosis: outcome, root cause, affected nodes, supporting symptoms, and evidence trail. Workload-centric means analyzing failures in the context of a workload rather than as isolated node events. Deterministic rules make the results reproducible and customizable, while structured output enables integration with existing health and recovery systems. NVIDIA health and resilience software helps teams keep AI workloads running. NVIDIA Attribution explains why a workload failed and provides evidence to guide the next action. It complements readiness checks, continuous health monitoring, and the systems that repair infrastructure and restart workloads. NVIDIA Attribution , the workload-centric failure-attribution system used across NVIDIA AI infrastructure, is open source. Used in production across NVIDIA AI infrastructure for years, NVIDIA Attribution analyzes millions of workloads each week across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. In one large RDMA-backed cluster, it correlated port errors, connection resets, and scheduler events to identify patterns around specific host and switch ports, helping teams target fabric repairs and congestion tuning. It includes two deployable components: the NVIDIA Attribution Service and the NVIDIA Attribution Blueprint; both components utilize a core attribution engine. The Service makes attribution available through a RESTAPI; the Blueprint connects cluster schedulers and telemetry sources to the Service and writes the result. Turn workload evidence into one diagnosis NVIDIA Attribution Service analyzes one workload attempt at a time. The Blueprint gathers the workload context and evidence, the Service extracts and correlates events, and the Blueprint returns a structured result. The path has four stages: Scope the workload. The Blueprint identifies the workload attempt from scheduler identifiers or from an explicit execution window and node allocation. Collect observations. Log and metric connectors produce workload-scoped Observation records from application logs, syslogs, GPU driver and Fabric Manager messages, scheduler history, node and network metrics. Extract and correlate events. The Service invokes the attribution engine to identify significant events such as GPU XIDs, NCCL failures, scheduler transitions, and metric conditions. Deterministic rules evaluate their timing and interaction, separate downstream symptoms from the event that caused the failure, and identify the root cause. Return a structured result. The Blueprint combines the verdict with the workload outcome ( terminal_state ), attributed domain ( sub_domain ), symptoms, affected nodes, and a record of collector coverage and errors. From applogs to attribution What follows is a worked example of extracting evidence, interpreting events, and preserving the symptoms that explain a distributed workload failure. Consider a multi-rank training workload in which one GPU encounters a hard fault e.g: XID 149 and NCCL errors follow across other ranks. NVIDIA Attribution correlates events across nodes, identifies the XID as the root cause, retains the NCCL failures in the symptom chain, and names the responsible node. The workload is reported as a hardware failure rather than a set of independent communication errors. A failed collective can leave error reports on several nodes. Those reports tell us where the workload noticed a problem. To explain the failure, NVIDIA Attribution combines them with evidence from other sources and evaluates the symptoms together. In this synthetic workload, application logs contain three different NCCL errors. System logs on node-02 contain XID 149 with error words that decode to NVLink signal integrity issue. We will follow that evidence through the rules pipeline. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market.
